item.content:encoded:
Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Users may have a constitutional right to access AI chatbot outputs. | Olivier Morin/AFP via Getty Images

There’s been a lot of concern over what AI chatbots communicate to users — from conversations that may encourage unhealthy emotional attachments, to advice on committing crimes.

Much of the debate over regulatory proposals and lawsuits concerning chatbots has focused on speech rights. There are open questions over whether outputs can be considered a form of legally protected speech.

Yet an overlooked aspect of these issues is the potential right of users to access chatbot outputs. The First Amendment protects not only the right to speak, but also the right to listen. Courts have found, for instance, that people have a right to receive mail from foreign propagandists and religious leaflets from proselytizers.

Some legal scholars say that figuring out how or whether to apply listeners’ rights to AI will be increasingly important to solve in the coming years, and may even become more significant than the speech issues in litigation.

Asserting free expression rights in this context is tricky because the First Amendment has traditionally applied to humans, rather than technology. By focusing on users, the argument becomes more straightforward since you’re focusing on human listeners.

“AI is a classic case of there might be an absent speaker, but listeners clearly are getting something meaningful in the sense the First Amendment cares about,” said Cornell tech law professor James Grimmelmann.

There have been some initial attempts to invoke listeners’ rights in cases concerning AI. In one case, litigants argued that the chatbot platform Character.AI should be required to prevent its AI companions from resembling real people or telling personal anecdotes. Character.AI responded that such an order would deprive users of their right to receive lifelike communications from its chatbots. The parties settled the case before the court could address the issue.

Listeners’ rights may eventually serve as a major barrier to those suing over the alleged mental health harms of chatbots. University of Florida tech and First Amendment law professor Jane Bambauer contends that listeners’ rights may be particularly strong when it comes to chatbots, because users are actively eliciting content.

“With a chatbot, if it's being used in a way where it's a constant interaction back and forth, then the listener may have a more active role in helping co-produce the output,” she told DFD. “In that sense, there would be a stronger listener rights argument that both the AI companies and the AI users would have.”

Grimmelmann notes, though, that the listeners’ rights argument may be somewhat weaker if a chatbot is encouraging suicide or is egregiously manipulative. He said, “All of these listener rights arguments take the listener's autonomy seriously, but they eventually, at some point, say … what you are doing is so harmful and so manipulative that you've effectively negated the autonomy.

Listeners’ rights may also be relevant to current controversies about the government limiting the release of powerful AI models like Fable. The justification for these restrictions is that the models have the potential to exploit previously unknown cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

Courts are often willing to circumscribe First Amendment rights when compelling national security interests are at stake. Yet these models aren’t only designed for cybersecurity — they can also engage in benign conversations with users. Law Reform Institute President Tim Schnabel suggests that wholesale prohibitions on the release of the models could deprive listeners from accessing a wide array of outputs.

“Fable was really good at legal policy analysis, and I wish I still had access to it,” he told DFD. “So to the extent that one buys that there are listeners' rights associated with using communicative tools like that, then the fact that it also has these cybersecurity capabilities is relevant, but doesn't negate the existence of the [First Amendment] aspects.”

item.title: When cheap AI becomes a secret weapon
item.description: When cheap AI becomes a secret weapon
item.content:encoded:
Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

The Chinese company Z.ai recently released a model with advanced cybersecurity capabilities. | Wang Zhao/AFP via Getty Images

China has once again put the U.S. AI industry on the defensive — not with the world’s smartest model, but with one that’s almost as capable as its American rivals at a fraction of the cost.

The Beijing-based company Z.ai released a model this month known as GLM-5.2, which security researchers say approaches the cybersecurity performance of leading U.S. models like Mythos, while costing roughly one-sixth as much. This lower price tag seems to be driving adoption, as GLM-5.2 has quickly become one of the top 10 most popular models in the world.

Z.ai’s model underscores that the AI race doesn’t solely come down to who has the most advanced model. Cheaper and more popular models could ultimately allow China to develop a stronger AI industry, which could have wide-ranging implications for competition with the U.S.

“Economic security is national security,” said New America senior fellow Samm Sacks. “The extent to which China is able to translate AI breakthroughs into economic gain and market share … does have a strategic impact on the balance of power.”

For years, U.S. AI companies have largely assumed that technological superiority would translate into commercial dominance. Models like GLM-5.2 may challenge that proposition.

“The OpenAIs, Anthropics and Googles of the world are mostly betting on proprietary models … you're using them essentially because they are the most intelligent,” said Sam Bresnick, an AI and national security research fellow at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. “That Chinese model now is considerably cheaper and almost as capable, and so it fundamentally threatens the business model of the proprietary developers.”

Even if the U.S. has the most advanced AI tech at the moment, the tables may turn if consumers flock to China’s cheaper alternatives. “Ultimately, if you lose the market, you will eventually lose the cutting edge, because you need that capital to keep pushing the frontier,” Hudson Institute senior fellow Bill Drexel told DFD.

Outsized profits for Chinese AI companies may mean they’ll have more capital and VC funding to develop frontier models that eventually surpass those in America. In that sense, the economics becomes increasingly intertwined with the national security imperatives of the AI race with China.

“If there's a future in which … a lot of the energy goes toward Chinese companies because they're cheaper, that leaves less money for [American] AI developers to continue innovating,” said Bresnick. “You get a scenario potentially in which there's less of a demand for that innovation, which leads the U.S. security apparatus and military to have fewer options and maybe a lack of technological superiority.”

There’s then a danger to excessively focusing on whether China or the U.S. has better AI cybersecurity tech. The fact that the American AI industry was the first to develop models like Mythos and GPT‑5.5‑Cyber proved a boon to national security, as the government could find and patch bugs in sensitive systems before anyone else had the tech. Yet that breathing room may shrink without the economics that allow U.S. frontier models to stay ahead.

“Economic power is increasingly hard to disentangle from traditional concepts of national security and national power,” Sacks told DFD.

There’s a possibility, however, that the U.S. will be able to sustain a technological lead long enough to allow its models to be the first to achieve recursive self-improvement — or AI that can exponentially advance itself.

“The theory is that if we hit recursive self-improvement, because the advancement will be so exponential, the functional difference of [being a few months ahead] will grow considerably and potentially be a serious head start,” said Drexel.

item.content:encoded:
Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Hassan Ali Kanu

Presented by 

With help from Aaron Mak

Social media's Big Tobacco moment hasn't come for AI. | Jenny Kane/AP

Liberal operatives behind the emerging “Project 2029” agenda argued earlier this week that social media and artificial intelligence are heading towards the same kind of legal reckoning that ultimately reshaped the Big Tobacco industry.

“In the 1990s, parents, states, courts, and the federal government came together to prevent cigarette companies from targeting kids,” the organizing group wrote in its framework for online child safety. “That same groundswell of opposition is now mobilizing against social media.” The pattern, it added, “is now repeating with chatbots”.

This comparison captures a growing consensus that courts will play a central role in regulating both industries. But, for now, the litigation facing AI companies remains fundamentally different from — and considerably less threatening than — the cases confronting social media.

Social media companies are fighting thousands of lawsuits brought by individuals, school districts and states, with much of that litigation consolidated into sprawling proceedings in California. Trials have already led to early consequences: a California jury in a bellwether trial held Meta and Google’s YouTube liable for negligent design, and YouTube reached a confidential settlement in a separate bellwether case. TikTok also reached a settlement in a separate case, according to Reuters, and the outcomes of all these proceedings could ultimately influence a broader settlement of claims in the consolidated litigation. 

Separately, a New Mexico judge is currently considering a range of additional penalties to force Meta to make its platforms safer. The company, meanwhile, has said that the judge’s forthcoming remedial orders may lead it to cease operations in New Mexico altogether.

By contrast, leading AI companies face far fewer consumer protection and product liability suits. A lawsuit filed by Florida against OpenAI earlier this month marked the first state consumer protection case targeting a major chatbot developer, but no comparable multistate coalition has yet emerged. That's due in part to the limited body of research documenting AI's psychological harms compared with the evidence surrounding social media, as well as Americans’ comparatively limited personal experience with the technology and its effects.

Instead, the AI industry's greatest legal risk lies in copyright. Statutory damages range from $750 to $30,000 per infringed work and can reach $150,000 for willful infringement, making the potential liability enormous. But even these high-stakes lawsuits have yet to pose a fundamental or existential threat to the business models of leading multi-billion-dollar AI companies.

More than 100 copyright lawsuits have been filed against leading AI developers by newspapers, book publishers, music companies and other rightsholders. Some plaintiffs have requested sweeping remedies. The New York Times' lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI, for example, asks a court to order the destruction of GPT models and training datasets that incorporate the newspaper's work.

Legal experts say that outcome is highly unlikely.

That would mean literally hitting the delete button on ChatGPT, much like deleting anything else housed on a computer or hard drives, according to Peter Henderson, a lawyer and assistant professor at Princeton University specializing in AI, machine learning and the intersection of law and policy.

The request “is more in the style of a wishlist than something the defendant would be particularly concerned about as a likely outcome,” said Joseph Petersen, a law partner at Kilpatrick Townsend whose work has involved landmark copyright cases. Petersen noted that judges are generally required to tailor relief to fit the circumstances of a case as narrowly as possible, a practice that makes orders more likely to survive appeal.

Courts can also order companies to implement technical guardrails — to modify or rebuild models with new parameters that minimize the possibility of the chatbot outputting verbatim or otherwise copyrighted material. And they can effectively direct companies to make their models “unlearn” certain information, although that remedy may be objectionable to plaintiffs because the process isn’t always effective, according to research by Henderson and others.

There are also the more familiar remedies — like money damages and negotiated licensing deals — that are more likely in the kinds of cases facing leading chatbot companies. Anthropic, for example, settled in September 2025 a copyright suit by a class of authors and publishers for $1.5 billion, covering roughly half a million works, with an estimated payout around $3,000 per eligible work. Universal Music Group last October announced that it settled copyright infringement claims against AI music creation platform Udio, including via a new licensing arrangement.

Taken together, those kinds of potential remedies certainly pose a threat to chatbot businesses. But even if the Big Tobacco analogy ultimately proves right, AI is still in an earlier chapter than social media. The latter is already confronting coordinated government litigation that challenges the legality of its core product design and represents a significant threat to current operations and business models. AI, for now, is mostly fighting over copyright infringement, which remains a more familiar legal problem for courts and business to address.

Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Programming note: We’ll be off this Friday, but will be back in your inboxes on Monday.

Ed Zitron | Handout.

Writer and podcaster Ed Zitron is the artificial intelligence boom’s most acerbic gadfly, known for his fervent criticism of the sector, which he says is undergirded by empty promises and shaky finances. Zitron also works as a public relations specialist for tech companies, putting him in the unusual position of being both a Silicon Valley insider and antagonist. He talks to us about the scourge of app notifications, and why Apple’s struggling Vision Pro augmented reality headset is on the right track.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Though the Vision Pro was about a decade too early, the idea of an expansive digital workspace is actually very cool. The Vision Pro was not a good product. What the Vision Pro would have to be to work was something bordering on weightless and invisible.

We've maxed out on the current interfaces. We've got mobile, we've got desktop and that's really it. So everyone wants to find the next computing place. The reason that a lot of people don't want to talk about this is that the actual way to get there is going to be a ton of investment in specialist hardware that is going to take a decade — it's going to take probably tens of billions of dollars in R&D.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

Generative AI is possibly the most overhyped technology of all time. It cannot do the things that we culturally think of when we think of AI. In general, we think of AI as this thing that's autonomous — set and forget it, invisible and it anticipates your needs.

Large language models are the literal opposite. You’re meant to have AI to mitigate your human errors. But by using generative AI you are just saying, “I've got to make sure that I monitor it for potential mistakes, add guardrails and all this crap around it so that it can be autonomous for me.” It's a giant con and it's frustrating because people try to conflate generative AI with regular machine learning and AlphaFold and other things that have shown some use. Generative AI has been hyped and connected to theoretical concepts and useful technology that do other things that are completely unrelated to it. That's how they sold all these GPUs for the data centers. They're claiming it's for AI writ large, when really it's for one specific kind of AI that is most decidedly not intelligent.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

They should regulate [phone] notifications like emissions. Look at how popups happen in apps. Your iPhone will be like, “Did you hear the Angels and the Marlins are playing?” I don't care! Duolingo has decided to harass you for the 15th time today. You used Abercrombie & Fitch's app once and now it's going to tell you every three days that it's got a sale on underwear.

The very concept of notifications has been turned into a form of manipulation by Meta and many other companies to the point that your phone is just covered in digital dirt — it's a mess. [The government] should regulate every notification and email sent by a company. We need to regulate them and say you can't use these for marketing or engagement — you can ask people to opt-in to the engagement, but it has to be strictly opt-in and it cannot be forced upon the user.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Financial Shenanigans by Howard Schilit. It's all about legal or quasi-legal accounting methods used by companies to make their earnings look better. It really shows you that tech companies are some of the biggest financial scammers in history. There's something about tech companies, because of the seeming complexity of their business, that allows them to just move numbers around to confuse investors.

Tech companies are able to twist the financial markets so much because they're not regulated properly. They are not forced into a place where they have to operate like normal businesses, which means that they do things to their customers that make the experience worse.

What has surprised you the most this year?

That the media is catching up to the AI bubble narrative. A year ago, they would speak about the AI bubble like it was some fringe belief. Now you look on every major news website and there's something about the AI bubble, and it's not discussed in theoretical terms anymore.

There was a lot of skepticism around the dotcom bubble, but there was a fairly early acceptance that it was a bubble as far as the telecommunication side goes. There weren't major media outlets that had columnists and podcasts that were singing the praises of these companies. There wasn't such an aggressive protection racket.

I've seen that protection racket start to fall apart [for AI]. The same outlets that were extremely pro-AI have started to say that perhaps the economics don't line up. I don't think they're fully conceptualizing how bad it's going to be yet, but it's good that we are finally having this discussion.

item.title: A business model for quantum computing
item.description: A business model for quantum computing
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

An IBM quantum computing system at the company's Thomas J. Watson Research Center in New York on June 6, 2025. | Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images

Researchers from the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Cleveland Clinic and IBM announced a breakthrough on Monday that could establish one of the first practical uses for quantum computing, a technology whose financial viability has long been a source of concern. The research team unveiled the first-known method for using AI-enhanced quantum computers to identify promising sources of tritium, a rare radioactive material needed to fuel future fusion reactors. The project may demonstrate how quantum computing can lead to discoveries that will be commercially valuable for renewable energy and other sectors. 

The announcement is part of the Genesis Mission — a federal initiative established in a November executive order to leverage frontier tech, like AI and quantum computing, to accelerate scientific discovery. DFD spoke with IBM’s director of research, Jay Gambetta, about how this project could help lay the groundwork for a quantum computing business model and the prospect of the industry sustaining itself without government support. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

Was quantum computing necessary to make this discovery? 

The teams are trying to solve a problem that matters for eventually creating fusion — this tritium production. I'm not going to say that quantum is required right now, but to get to the point where we can scale this, you're not going to be able to solve it with classical [computing]. The way I look at this is the first significant step where we can actually show a workflow that runs on a quantum computer, runs on classical supercomputers and runs using AI.

What role did the Genesis Mission play in this research?

I think of it as a partnership. From the IBM side, we obviously understand quantum computers. We are not experts in nuclear fusion. [The Genesis Mission is] forcing a collaboration to do things that are beyond what a single institution could do. It was coordinating the expertise and the ambition.

One of the concerns with the Genesis Mission is that the government has separately cut back on a lot of the data collection operations that could help with research. How have you found the process of finding the necessary data for your research? 

One of the beautiful things with quantum is it's not something that's driven by data. What we're doing is looking at the problem in a way where data doesn't exist for those types of solutions. Quantum gives us the accuracy to allow us to make predictions that we can't make from previous data.

Based on how this research project was structured, what do you see as the business model for quantum computing?

The business model is very simple at the moment. We want to build quantum computers and provide [customers] with capacity. Obviously, in this experiment we worked with the national labs, but we also have over 370 members of what we call our IBM Quantum Network — that includes commercial clients who are already looking at using quantum computers. So this is just one example of us going from toy problems to practical problems. And then eventually our business model is through [providing] the capacity of using our systems.

So the business model would be, say, a fusion company presenting you with a problem to be solved with your quantum computing service?

Yes. And of course, the customers … in this case are some of the best nuclear physicists on the planet. They need to know the exact problem to a [precise] degree. I can give you my best answer as a physicist [with] my university degree, but what I know best is the quantum computing side. Once we take their idea, we know how to really map it efficiently onto our quantum computers. That's why the partnership between experts who really understand their domain and us, as experts who understand quantum computing, allows us to iterate much faster.
Spanberger bucks data center moratorium

Democratic Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger is pushing back against a proposed nationwide moratorium on data center construction that’s becoming increasingly popular in her party, POLITICO’s Josh Siegel reports.

On the Monday episode of the POLITICO Energy podcast, Spanberger said “walking away from the table” to implement the moratorium would threaten economic growth and national security. Spanberger’s state has the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and she said a national pause on new construction would have “a major impact on jobs in Virginia, union jobs, electrical jobs, certainly the building trades.” She added, “The need for data centers, processing of information, there's a national security implication here in Virginia. We don't, as a nation, want to cede that ground.”

Instead, Spanberger, a former CIA intelligence officer who ran on making energy more affordable, said communities should have more say in deciding where data centers are located. Spanberger’s rebuttal was in response to Energy and Commerce Committee ranking member Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) endorsing a moratorium in June.
Supreme Court allows Texas to enforce app age verification

The Supreme Court denied a request to temporarily block Texas’s age verification law for app stores on Monday, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp and Hassan Ali Kanu report.

The ruling effectively means the state can enforce its Texas App Store Accountability Act — which requires app stores to implement age verification measures and obtain parental consent for minors downloading apps — while a First Amendment challenge to the law from the Youth advocacy organization Students Engaged in Advancing Texas and the Computer & Communications Industry Association proceeds in the lower courts. The Supreme Court’s one-sentence order did not explain the decision.

CCIA President Matt Schruers said his association looks forward “to an expedited hearing before the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in early August to demonstrate how Texas’ App Store Accountability Act violates the First Amendment.” SEAT and the office of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, which is defending the law, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Hollywood's AI habits become courtroom evidence
item.description: Hollywood's AI habits become courtroom evidence
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The generative AI company Midjourney is defending against a copyright lawsuit from major entertainment studios. | Mario Tama/Getty Images

The generative AI company Midjourney is turning Hollywood’s own AI ambitions into a legal defense.

Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. filed lawsuits last year alleging that the use of their content to train Midjourney’s image generator constitutes copyright infringement.

As part of its defense, Midjourney is attempting to prove that the studios are also taking advantage of AI trained on other people’s work. The company won a partial court order in June forcing the studios to disclose how they use AI to create content released to consumers. In a motion filed last week, Midjourney asked the court to also make the studios produce information on how AI may be used internally for storyboarding or coming up with content ideas.

If the studios are working with AI tools like Midjourney’s platform — and that’s a big if — the ramifications may extend well beyond the bad optics of hypocrisy. The finding could establish that using AI in this manner is an industry standard. If an increasing number of courts come to similar conclusions, it could potentially send ripples through the entertainment and tech economies.

“If more and more content is going to be produced with this technology and this technology is going to train on everything, then what we're going to end up with is just a regression of synthetic content,” said Vered Horesh, chief AI strategy officer at Bria — a generative AI platform that’s exclusively trained on licensed works.

Midjourney’s primary argument is that training AI on unlicensed content constitutes fair use, a legal exception that allows for the appropriation of copyrighted works for limited purposes in a transformative fashion.

To determine whether something falls within the fair use exception, courts will sometimes consider what’s custom for a certain industry. Basically if everyone is doing the same thing, then it could be an indicator that the industry broadly thinks it’s reasonable.

Emory AI law professor Matthew James Sag suggests, for example, that it’s common practice to quote works of copyrighted literature in biographies of authors — not only is it transformative, but there’s also a general consensus that it’s fair and customary. Midjourney is essentially trying to demonstrate that there’s a similar custom for AI trained on copyrighted content, and even asserted in a brief that many of its subscribers are associated with corporate email addresses from Disney and Universal.

“You could introduce evidence [demonstrating]: ‘Hey, this person is suing us for infringement. They do exactly the same thing that we are, within the bounds of accepted practice,’” Sag told DFD.

This kind of evidence wouldn’t necessarily be a silver bullet for Midjourney by itself. And though this AI copyright case has been getting a lot of attention, it’s only one of many working through the courts.

Yet if courts start generally accepting the idea that everyone in the entertainment and tech industries is training AI on copyrighted works or using the resulting tools, and they broadly agree that it’s transformative, there could be wide-ranging impacts.

“If the courts come out and say this is highly transformative … then that's kind of telling us that this practice is consistent with a broader social judgment that this is just where the limits of copyright are and it's not actually unfair,” said Sag, who added that a win for Midjourney would likely cause the entertainment industry to “start leaning into AI a bit more.”

Horesh fears that allowing Hollywood and Silicon Valley to rely on AI training unrestrained by copyright would result in reduced incentives for the kinds of human-made content that’s needed to develop the technology itself. “If we eliminate all incentives for human creation, because we don't include human creators in the AI value chain, then we are not going to have any human-created content,” she said. “At some point this is going to also affect the quality of the generative models themselves.”

Midjourney declined to comment. Disney, Warner Bros. and Universal did not respond to inquiries.
ABC hits back at Carr

ABC admonished Federal Communications Chair Brendan Carr in a Tuesday filing for accusing the network of mounting “a campaign of misinformation,” POLITICO’s John Hendel reports.

ABC submitted the filing to defend “The View” amid FCC proceedings to determine whether the program should continue to be exempt from rules requiring networks to give competing candidates equal airtime. ABC pointed to comments that tens of thousands of people submitted to the FCC advocating for “The View” to have latitude over the guests it books.

“The commenters are right to be concerned,” ABC said in the filing. “The First Amendment does not permit the government to sit in an editor’s chair.” The network launched an ad campaign in June calling on viewers to submit their input to the FCC. “I do think Disney is running a campaign of misinformation here,” Carr recently told reporters. “Most specifically, one of the things I saw is this statement from them in this ad campaign that the FCC is trying to control who can appear on the show. … That’s not consistent with what the law provides.”
EU pushes for global AI benchmarking

The European Union wants its system for testing AI models’ cybersecurity risks to be used globally, POLITICO’s Sam Clark and Pieter Haeck report.

In response to concerns about the hacking abilities of powerful AI models like Mythos, the EU formulated an action plan earlier this year to allow certain companies to access and evaluate the cybersecurity capabilities of frontier models before they’re released in the European market.

European Commission Executive Vice President for tech and cyber policy Henna Virkkune told POLITICO on Tuesday that the bloc wants its plan to become a “global benchmark” for testing models and deciding which companies should get preliminary access. She also contended that there is no equivalent framework anywhere else in the world.

item.title: Washington’s quantum reality check
item.description: Washington’s quantum reality check
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The White House held a quantum innovation summit on Tuesday. | White House handout.

Quantum is in the air in Washington. 

The White House held a summit with quantum companies on Tuesday to discuss innovation in the sector. IBM, PsiQuantum, D-Wave and Quantinuum told DFD that they were among the companies present.

An attendee, granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door event, said it was “standing-room only” with well over 100 people joining. The person called it “probably the most crowded quantum summit of its kind.”

The interest in the summit may reflect how aggressively the administration has approached quantum over the past two months. The Department of Commerce announced in May that it plans to provide more than $2 billion in incentives to support nine quantum-focused companies. In late June, President Donald Trump signed two executive orders aimed at boosting quantum development and preparing federal systems for quantum-enabled cyberattacks.

Following the flurry of government initiatives last year to support the AI buildout, the administration has been expanding its innovation agenda to support other emerging technologies like robotics and quantum computing.

A critical component of the quantum efforts that hasn’t gotten as many headlines is the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency program to determine whether it would be possible to build an industrially useful quantum computer by 2033. The summit attendee told DFD that the initiative was a major topic of discussion — with Undersecretary of Defense Emil Michael attesting to its rigor in particular.

QBI is meant to cut through industry hype, and its findings could ultimately shape the U.S.’s quantum strategy and investment in the sector. “This industry is full of big personalities and big claims,” the attendee told DFD. “There is a really important role for DARPA in putting those claims to the test.”

QBI is specifically examining the feasibility of building “utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers” — or in other words, quantum computers that are cost-effective and can operate despite computational and hardware imperfections.

DARPA has previously signaled that it’s taking a hard-nosed approach to the benchmarking initiative. Joe Altepeter, the founding program manager of QBI, said during a December conference that the agency is fully prepared to accept that developing an industrially useful quantum computer won’t be possible in the next seven years.

“Our job is to prevent surprise and give ground truth to the U.S. government to make wise decisions,” Altepeter told the crowd at a December quantum industry conference. “And we are perfectly fine if the answer is: ‘No one’s going to be able to build this. We should spend our money building giant robots or curing cancer instead — don't worry about quantum computing.’”

Yet there’s a lot riding on quantum computing, as the technology is expected to eventually make modern encryption methods obsolete and unlock major advancements in energy and medicine. And as with AI, there’s industry and government concern that China’s quantum tech will pull ahead.

Given the stakes, Software & Information Industry Association global public policy and government affairs head Paul Lekas thinks the U.S.’s quantum efforts will still have momentum even if QBI determines that the 2033 timeline isn’t feasible.

“You're going to continue to see interest … because of all the potential applications as well as the concerns that if the United States doesn't get there first, we are potentially vulnerable to what potential adversarial actors can do with those capabilities,” Lekas told DFD. “I don't think you're going to see scientists and the private sector and government say, ‘OK we're going to pause what we're doing right now and wait.’”

What’s more, 2033 isn’t a hard-and-fast deadline. DARPA has suggested that it’s open to working with companies that aim to achieve this feat by 2036 instead. According David Bernal Neira, a Purdue University chemical engineering professor who studies quantum, there’s a general consensus that building such a computer is possible — it’s just a matter of when.

“I see [QBI] as an accelerator and as a field for an already ongoing competition to happen, whether or not the goals are achieved by the deadline that has been set,” he told DFD. “If this goalpost of 2033 is not achieved, I still think that we will be at a stage that is much, much closer than where we are right now.”

 The results of QBI could meaningfully affect government and support and private investment, by validating some companies’ approaches to developing a viable quantum computer, and rejecting others.

“if DARPA eventually comes back and says this method that this company is exploring seems to work … then that would help to raise further investment,” said Lekas. “If DARPA were to say that there's a method that they think has no chance at all of actually achieving this goal … then that's going to make things challenging for the companies that are adopting that method.”

One of Trump’s June executive orders also indicated that information from QBI will also inform how the government builds out supply chains for quantum computer hardware, which the summit attendee said administration officials emphasized as a main focus for implementing the recent executive orders. Neira noted that supply chains may need to be tailored to a whichever approaches QBI determines to be viable — for instance, some approaches rely heavily on lasers while others require more cooling equipment or helium.

Neira told DFD, “When you go into the question of what it means for them to be at the utility scale … that's a supply chain question.”

A DARPA spokesperson said, "QBI’s goal is to provide the U.S. government with the best possible assessment of the current state of commercial quantum computing and its likely trajectory, so that those stakeholders can make informed decisions. ... While not guaranteed, QBI estimates that on balance, it is more likely than not that at least one company will be able to create an industrially useful quantum computer by 2033."

The Pentagon and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy did not respond to inquiries.
OpenAI will release its most powerful model

OpenAI announced late Tuesday that it will release its advanced GPT-5.6 models after holding off at the request of the Trump administration, POLITICO’s Katherine Long reports.

The company said in the announcement that the models — named Luna, Sol and Terra — will be available to customers globally on Thursday. The administration requested that OpenAI stagger the release of the models last month to allow for testing of their powerful capabilities by the government and a small group of trusted partners.

An OpenAI spokesperson told POLITICO that it has been working with the White House and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation to preview and test GPT-5.6 for more than a month, with meetings dating back to CEO Sam Altman’s visit with the White House and lawmakers on June 3.
Online safety advocates slam the White House

The family of a 17-year-old who died by suicide after being sexually extorted on Instagram is condemning a White House intervention that saved top tech executives from having to testify before Congress, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp reports.

Tania and Tim Woods, who are backing the James T. Woods Act that’s named after their deceased son, raised their objections in a Wednesday letter obtained by POLITICO to Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), other committee members and the White House. The pair criticized the White House’s deal with Grassley to support the legislation, aimed at combating online exploitation of young users, in exchange for allowing lower-level Meta and Google executives to testify before the committee rather than their CEOs.

“It was our understanding that this legislation was never intended to become a political bargaining chip,” the letter reads. “It was created because children have died.” Grassley’s press secretary Hannah Akey said, “The James T. Woods Act is a hugely bipartisan and widely supported bill that tackles disgusting crimes harming children nationwide … [Chairman Grassley] will continue his ongoing investigations of Big Tech, while also passing laws that will protect children across America.”

Meta, Durbin and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: The tricky business of AI cloning
item.description: The tricky business of AI cloning
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

AI clones of deceased people are becoming increasingly common. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

Generative AI has become a powerful tool for distilling a person’s legacy in digital form.

Training AI on a person’s biographical information, statements and recordings can create lifelike digital clones that people can talk with even after someone’s death. The technology is becoming increasingly common: visitors at the National WWII Museum can interact with clones of veterans, and an emerging “grief tech” industry is leveraging AI to let people converse with deceased loved ones.

But what if you don’t want your persona to be encapsulated by an AI clone after you pass away, or if you want to set ground rules for how your clone is used?

This is where the right of publicity may come into play, which is a legal protection that gives people control over how their voice, likeness and image are appropriated. States like California and Texas have long had laws for a post-mortem right of publicity, though they weren’t designed with AI in mind.

Determining whether — and how — a person can control their AI clones from beyond the grave involves contentious debates over dignity, commercial exploitation and a potentially dystopian future. Though this cloning technology is relatively new, legal scholars told DFD that questions relating to the technology will become more urgent.

“Given how technology has evolved, we really need to protect the dead because they are the one group who can never [correct it],” said University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill tech and intellectual property professor Dustin Marlan.

One of the difficulties with applying a post-mortem right of publicity to AI clones is that the protection has traditionally been aimed at commercial uses of a person’s likeness. As a result, it has mainly benefitted people whose likeness has commercial value — think celebrities, artists and entertainers. Existing laws generally regulate the use of their likenesses for ads or merchandise.

The likenesses of most ordinary people don't have commercial value, so post-mortem rights of publicity aren’t often invoked on their behalf. In practice, that means non-celebrities have few legal tools for setting terms on AI clones that may be generated after they die.

Emma Perot, an intellectual property law professor at the University of the West Indies at St. Augustine, suggests that the advent of AI should prompt legislators to rethink likeness protections.

“The ability to exploit someone after death used to be a lot more limited,” Perot told DFD. “It's only now that regular people are really becoming more susceptible, because regular people can be cloned in this very accurate manner.”

One way to expand post-mortem publicity rights beyond commercial contexts, according to Perot, would be to reconceive them as privacy protections. While publicity rights for living people are intended in part to safeguard privacy, the law has historically viewed privacy as less important for the deceased.

“There's some consideration that you might have this privacy interest even after death due to how accurately AI can replicate you,” said Perot.

The NO FAKES Act, which advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee last month, incorporates such considerations. The act provides all people, whether public figures or private citizens, with a right to their likenesses. That right would last for 70 years after one’s death.

One ambiguity in the NO FAKES Act and similar state laws has to do with exceptions allowing for the use of someone’s likeness for commentary or criticism. So, while selling unauthorized merchandise with Elvis Presley’s face is legally suspect in some states, making a biopic about him fits more comfortably into the exception. Marlan says it’s unclear whether an AI clone could be considered a form of commentary on the person in certain cases.

“There are gray areas that you really do need to see litigated, assuming the [NO FAKES Act] does pass,” he told DFD.

Another possible solution is for AI cloning companies to establish industry standards. Alex Quinn, CEO of the AI digital twin company Authentic Interactions, says around 30 percent of their projects involve replicating someone who’s already died. Quinn himself created a clone of his dad, who passed away when he was a child.

“We would like to help create some type of standard where there can be a go-to set of rules on how stuff like that operates,” said Quinn, who added it could help establish an “opt-in or opt-out” mechanism for people to confirm whether they want to be digitally cloned after dying. At the moment, however, Quinn is relying on his own sense of what’s ethical to do with the technology. For instance, he’s generally averse to creating clones for marketing purposes.

“I'm not in the dead person advertising business,” he told DFD.
Nexstar-Tegna notch a temporary win in DC

The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed a challenge Thursday to the Federal Communications Commission’s approval of Nexstar and Tegna’s $6.2 billion merger, POLITICO’s John Hendel reports.

The court found the conservative cable company Newsmax, public interest groups, DirecTV and other challengers brought the suit too early, noting the FCC’s commissioners have not yet reviewed the approval, which came out of the agency’s Media Bureau. “This court therefore lacks jurisdiction over appellants’ challenges and must dismiss the consolidated appeals,” the court wrote in the order.

Nexstar and Tegna are still fighting an antitrust challenge to the merger in California federal court. The D.C. Circuit’s order also does not prevent the challengers from refiling once the FCC reviews the application, which is expected sometime this year.
California to get $2.9 million from Block settlement

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a $45 million multistate settlement with Cash App’s parent company, Block, on Wednesday, POLITICO’s California Decoded team reports.

Dozens of attorneys general sued Block for allegedly misleading consumers about the safety of Cash App and failing to prevent fraud. The officials accused Block of maintaining lax identity-verification measures for account setup and encouraging people without traditional bank accounts to rely on Cash App. California is set to receive $2.9 million from the settlement.

“Block told Cash App customers that their money was just as safe and secure as in a bank — which is not true — and then left its customers high and dry when things went wrong. Consumers were stranded: unable to access their money, vulnerable to scammers, and without any recourse or even a phone number to call when they found themselves victims of fraud,” Bonta said in a statement. Block did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: 5 Questions for Eugenio Battaglia
item.description: 5 Questions for Eugenio Battaglia
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Eugenio Battaglia | Handout.

Eugenio Battaglia is a biotechnology researcher who has worked with the European Union to develop frameworks for responsible synthetic biology, and with the United Nations to design digital platforms for achieving its Sustainable Development Goals. Battaglia is now a Future Fellow at Evermay, a nonprofit that supports the development of ideas that benefit humanity, where he is developing a “Large Moral Model” designed to understand the nuances of ethical dilemmas. He talks to us about what the AI safety and accelerationism debate overlooks, and the misplaced priorities of frontier labs. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Most AI alignment work has quietly sidestepped questions around whose values get prioritized, and whose dissent gets excluded when a model resolves a disagreement into a single flat answer. Current frontier labs tend to prioritize proficiency of their models in domains such as STEM or corporate tasks, while resorting to simplify the hard problems of morality into flat, pre-baked answers that reflect the basin of a generic, mostly Western, politically-correct thinking.

[At Evermay], I’ll be working on a language model that is trained to have a much more nuanced understanding of moral complexity, one that is rooted in a wide representation of moral views across global cultures. I call this a Large Moral Model. The ability to hold the paradoxes and complexity of moral disagreement without necessarily reaching consensus is an underrated big idea in democracy, and so it’s an urgent one in the development of artificial intelligence models.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

Context engineering [the practice of curating the information provided to AI models to optimize performance]. Context engineering is the bleeding edge of the honestly sloppy conversation happening on LinkedIn or X these days. People are drinking the kool-aid of miraculous harnesses and agentic pipelines that are promising to solve … the reliability of agents. Yes it is entertaining and fun to follow what people are trying to hack around, but there’s a better way of using our time.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

The government is currently trapped in a narrow dichotomy: either regulate AI for safety, or treat it as a commercial arms race. It is missing the far more critical role of acting as the architect of a digital commons. We need to evolve our public institutions — specifically libraries and public broadcasters — into 21st-Century knowledge utilities. Today, these institutions are often retreating to physical materials because publishers block digital access. Governments should fund the "plumbing" of these digital commons.

This means supporting the technical pipelines that help local, trusted institutions convert their internal archives into clean, public datasets, rather than letting proprietary cloud providers become the sole gatekeepers of our collective cultural record.

The government should foster a "knowledge utility" model where public-interest data — such as archival mission records or local public media — is made … high-quality for training as a baseline public good. By treating this data as foundational infrastructure rather than just "content," governments can ensure that AI development doesn't rely solely on enclosing the public record. This creates a "multiverse" of public and open-source models that can operate independently of big tech centralization, serving the cultural and educational needs of the public rather than just the profit margins of model labs.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Belly by Nora Bateson and Steps to an Ecology of the Mind by Gregory Bateson. Both moved me from a world of separable things to a world of relations that has gently reframed my view of the future as something living to be tended rather than a machine to be optimized.

What has surprised you the most this year?

How much the alignment conversation has shifted from "how do we make models more capable" to "how do we make models capable of holding the complexity of our world." A year ago this was almost entirely about guardrails and rule-following, and to a certain extent it still is. Now there's more appetite for models across the board that can sit with unresolved tension, that can be useful in contexts that were normally highly policed.
EU marshals research for social media ban

An expert assessment of social media’s impact on children that could fuel efforts for a ban in the European Union is set to be released on Monday, POLITICO’s Eliza Gkritsi and Gabriel Gavin report.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen recruited dozens of experts specializing in fields like child psychiatry and social epidemiology to produce a report on how the EU can protect young users from online harms. Von der Leyen has previously asserted that social media is damaging to kids and called for EU-wide restrictions on platforms. An EU official said that the report is aimed at providing “an evidence base” to convince skeptical national governments to support any proposals for a social media ban.

Von der Leyen is expected to publicly accept the report’s findings on Monday. An official who has viewed the report told POLITICO that it stops short of specifying what should be banned.
Khanna raises alarm about White House app

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) implored the White House to pause the use of a government app due to potential cybersecurity threats from China in a Thursday letter first obtained by POLITICO’s Maggie Miller.

The White House launched the app, which provides updates on President Donald Trump’s policies and executive actions, in March and pushed to have it installed on federal devices. In his letter, Khanna cited reports that the app includes software from the Shenzhen-based telecommunications company Huawei.

“The White House should not be violating Americans’ data privacy, and it certainly should not expose them to potential intelligence collection by foreign governments,” Khanna wrote.

item.title: AI is giving election conspiracies a new playbook
item.description: AI is giving election conspiracies a new playbook
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Owen Dahlkamp

With help from Aaron Mak

Local officials say AI was used in an attempt to influence California's June primary. | Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images

The midterms are shaping up to be a major test of how artificial intelligence can influence American democracy.

Election officials and misinformation researchers are increasingly worried that generative AI could produce convincingly fake audio, photos and videos that supercharge claims of voter fraud. They fear, in particular, the technology will be used to create false evidence in support of conspiracy theories and raise questions about ballot counting.

Audio and visual evidence “is so much more effective in terms of making people believe a manufactured reality” compared to assertions made without so-called evidence, said Bhaskar Chakravorti, a dean and misinformation researcher at Tufts University.

Officials are already seeing attempts to use the technology to influence elections in the wild. Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan said AI was used during California’s June primaries to manipulate publicly-available videos to fuel claims of fraud as officials tallied the results. The experience is prompting some officials to rethink how much election footage they make available, even as they try to maintain transparency.

There’s also growing concern about what information AI models access. As publishers increasingly restrict access to their content, models could rely more heavily on less authoritative sources such as Reddit and LinkedIn, according to former Facebook public policy director Katie Harbath. This could make it easier for bad actors to inundate these sites with false information that could be picked up by AI, said Harbath, who now advises election officials through her technology consulting firm Anchor Change.

That risk could be especially acute as the public awaits election results, a period when conspiracy theories could percolate, especially if the counting process drags on. Harbath told POLITICO she has advised hundreds of election officials nationwide to publish explainers on audits, recounts and other routine processes before Election Day so both voters and AI systems have access to reliable information when questions arise.

David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, said such explanatory content could help with prebunking — distributing information ahead of the election that proactively bats down common conspiracies, like widespread noncitizen voting or alleged hacking of voting machines.

Foreign influence operations that exploit the technology remain another concern. Todd Helmus, founder of advisory firm Meridian Influence Group, expects Russia and China to use AI to meddle in elections and to sow distrust.

Still, some election experts, like Becker, argue false claims from political elites remain a far more powerful driver of election misinformation than the technology itself. “I do not believe AI is radically changing the misinformation environment,” he said. “That’s largely because the disinformation environment was already so difficult.”
A new little tech trade group

More than 200 startups, growth-stage companies and investors are launching a new trade group called the Little Tech Association to check the market power of Big Tech, POLITICO’s Gabby Miller was the first to report.

The Little Tech Association — whose members include Yelp and Y Combinator — will promote “robust antitrust enforcement and targeted reforms” to update competition policy, according to a fact sheet. The group aims to counteract Big Tech’s recent moves to bulk up its political influence via K Street and its connections with the Trump administration.

“As AI reshapes the economy, [the Little Tech Association] will fight to keep it open and competitive so the best ideas win on merit," said Harry Godfrey, the group’s founding executive director, in a statement to POLITICO.
EU sanctions Russian hacking group

The European Union is imposing sanctions on a range of individuals and entities that it says has been tied to hacking activities by Russia's Federal Security Service, POLITICO’s Émile Marzolf, Antoaneta Roussi, Jonas Loesel and Sam Clark report.

In a Monday announcement, the European Council accused the FSB of directing cybercriminals, companies and state-backed hacking groups like Turla to launch cyberattacks across the European Union and Ukraine since 2010. The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot also said during a Monday BFMTV appearance that France will summon the Russian ambassador over the hacking operations.

“These operations target military personnel, companies and operators and are intended either to intercept communications or to sabotage operations,” Barrot said.

item.title: Cities enter the AI debate
item.description: Cities enter the AI debate
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

New York City has a law requiring audits for AI hiring systems. | Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images

One of the most contentious sticking points in the national debate over artificial intelligence is the extent to which states rather than the federal government should be able to regulate the technology.

But a growing number of cities are also asserting their own authority over AI. Last week, Rockville became the first city in Maryland to prohibit the use of AI for setting rental costs. San Francisco has a similar ban in place, and New York City requires bias audits for AI that helps make employment decisions. Overall, more than 20 U.S. cities and counties have instituted their own policies regarding the technology.

In some ways, it makes sense for cities to have a say — local governments may be more intimately aware of how technology is affecting people on the ground level, and they can often act faster than state or federal policymakers. At the same time, AI industry boosters already complain that companies must navigate a patchwork of state laws. City AI policies could create another patchwork across states.

“There's value in having a unified national market or international market, and then there's also value in allowing regulation to be tailored to local concerns,” Yale urban law professor David Schleicher told DFD. “There are deep trade-offs between those things.”

States ultimately determine what local governments can regulate, which is laid out in municipal charters that establish cities. Existing charters don’t provide specific grants of authority over AI, but they cover issues like transportation or housing.

Municipal governments have sought to regulate technology when it impacts an area of policy that’s traditionally been within their purview. Schleicher told DFD, “Cities have regulated certain policy areas, and much of their intervention into the internet has been about regulating those policy areas as internet companies came into them.” For example, cities have imposed rules on rideshare platforms like Uber, as they’ve long regulated taxi services.

Localities have more authority to oversee “the conditions on how AI is being used, either for delivering local services, or for a few areas like employment and education that might have been delegated to cities,” said Stefaan Verhulst, co-founder of New York University’s Governance Laboratory. A city where an autonomous car company is headquartered wouldn’t be able to dictate how self-driving models are developed, but might be able to prohibit the vehicles from operating on local roads.

There are, however, plenty of arguments for limiting cities’ oversight of AI. Patchwork regulation could stifle AI innovation if companies have to navigate a maze of both state and municipal rules. Cities also often don’t have staff with technical expertise to truly understand how to regulate AI.

On the flipside, preventing cities from having their own AI policies could dampen democratic input. “[Cities] can do better participatory AI governance, meaning that they can actually consult with communities and their residents in ways that give a signal on what their expectations are as it relates to the use of AI,” Verhulst told DFD. “States can do this as well, of course, but cities are much closer to their residents than states are, let alone the federal government.”

That input may be valuable in the case of AI, as its benefits and costs often aren’t distributed evenly across the country. Data centers support AI systems being used nationwide, but impacts from the facilities will be felt by the community living next to it. “AI is one of those phenomena where the people who benefit don't live in the same places as the people who pay the costs,” said Aaron Saiger, faculty director of the Fordham Urban Law Center. “So part of the question is how to deal with that situation where there is a benefit in a broad geographic constituency and then localized costs.”
European Union relaxes smart glasses rules

The European Commission announced on Tuesday it will exempt wearable devices from a rule requiring products to have removable batteries, POLITICO’s Ellen O'Regan and Mathieu Pollet report.

The change removes a major barrier for Meta’s ambitions to expand its smart glasses business to Europe. The U.S. has been pressuring the EU to change the rule.

U.S. Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder said during a Meta event in March that the bloc’s regulations were “so broad and so restrictive that it prevents the sale of this wonderful, jointly developed, U.S.-European product from being sold in the European Union.” Puzder also called the glasses “very stylish” and “very wonderful.”

A European Commission spokesperson said in a statement that it “has not given in to anyone’s pressure” in making the policy change. The spokesperson also contended that the commission’s proposals “follow a broad public consultation with consumer associations, industry stakeholders and the Member States.” Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Deepmind calls for an AI standards body

DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis proposed in an essay Tuesday that the U.S. establish a body for testing frontier AI models and setting standards for the technology, POLITICO’s Frank Hersey reports.

Hassabis suggested that the body could be industry-funded and modeled on public-private regulators, much like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. He also wrote that the body should be overseen by a board that includes leading independent tech experts, including those from the open-source space. Similar to provisions in President Donald Trump’s June executive order for frontier model testing, Hassabis’s proposed body would review models that AI companies voluntarily submit 30 days prior to public release.

Hassabis’s proposal resembles one that OpenAI’s Sam Altman presented in a Financial Times op-ed published in early July. Altman, however, called for the creation of a U.S.-led international forum while Hassabis’s proposed body would focus on domestic oversight.

item.title: Why click-to-cancel is a crowdpleaser
item.description: Why click-to-cancel is a crowdpleaser
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Brendan Bordelon

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has aggressively promoted a new click-to-cancel rule. | Seth Wenig/AP

Over the past week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has raced go-karts, brandished a Chinese finger trap and delivered remarks in front of ellipticals to trumpet a new click-to-cancel rule — which requires companies to make canceling a subscription online as easy as it is to sign up for one.

While it hasn’t exuded the same zany panache, the Federal Trade Commission also touted settlements secured against companies like Amazon and Shutterstock relating to allegedly complicated cancellation processes. Chris Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, highlighted online subscriptions as one of three priority areas for his division in a March speech. A bipartisan group of House lawmakers reintroduced a click-to-cancel bill in January as well.

Measures to ensure easy cancellation of online subscriptions has become a crowdpleaser in tech policy. Though state and federal laws regulating cancellations have been on the books for years, the rising importance of kitchen-table issues has renewed interest in the topic from regulators.

“I think certainly there is something different about this moment,” said John Breyault, vice president for public policy and fraud at the National Consumers League. “Consumers and their [representatives] in Washington and around the country are more aware than ever about the tricks and traps that contribute to the affordability crisis.”

Despite a degree of bipartisan appeal over policing online subscription cancellations, views vary across the political spectrum. The Mamdani administration, for example, has focused on the implications of this policy for his affordability agenda.

“From the day that he launched his campaign, Mayor Mandani promised New Yorkers that making this city more affordable would be the north star of his administration,” former FTC Chair Lina Khan, who helped lead Mamdani’s transition team, said during a Friday press conference on the new click-to-cancel rule. She added, “Some of the richest companies in our economy now treat subscription tricks and traps as a systemic way to squeeze more and more money out of Americans.” New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection Commissioner Sam Levine, another Biden FTC alum who proposed the rule in March, also spoke of affordability during the conference.

In his various speeches and statements on online cancellations this year, Mufarrige has generally framed it as a matter of economic liberty. In the FTC’s announcement on the Shutterstock settlement, he said complicated cancellation processes “deprive consumers of the ability to make informed choices, undermining consumer sovereignty and impeding competition.”

The Trump FTC’s approach is somewhat more conventional than New York City’s. Under Khan, the Biden-era FTC issued a click-to-cancel rule similar to Mamdani’s, though the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals struck it down last year on procedural grounds. New York City’s click-to-cancel rule reflects Khan’s expansive approach to consumer protection in some respects, imposing stricter requirements than similar regulations elsewhere in the country.

“New York [City’s] rule is definitely the one that we hold up along with California’s as being really the gold standard when it comes to click-to-cancel rules,” said Breyault, pointing in particular to the rigorous consumer compensation and civil penalty provisions.

The Trump FTC has taken a less expansive approach than Khan’s, relying on the 2010 Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act to address difficult online cancellations. “The current FTC has placed less emphasis on rulemaking and more emphasis on enforcement where there is clear statutory authority, in this case under ROSCA,” Chris Bissex, a former FTC communications official from Trump’s second term, told DFD. When discussing online subscriptions in his March speech, Mufarrige said, “Rather than focus on novel applications of the law, we are focused on enforcing the statutes that Congress has specifically charged us with.”

Yet the FTC hasn’t taken new online subscription rules completely off the table. The agency announced an advance notice of proposed rulemaking in March, indicating that it’s pursuing click-to-cancel regulations once again. However, it remains to be seen how much that rule will resemble those from New York City or the Biden-era FTC. Current FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson voted against the Biden-era rule when he was a commissioner.

Kelley Drye & Warren Partner Gonzalo Mon said the notice suggests that the new rule will have a lot of the same basic elements as the one that was struck down, though there may be differences in terms of scope and exemptions.

“The [notice] covers many of the same issues and themes of the Biden-era rule, though with some new questions and a difference in tone, language and branding,” he told DFD. “The core of the proposal is similar: prohibiting misrepresentations, requiring disclosure of material terms, obtaining express informed consent and providing a simple cancellation mechanism.”

Amazon directed DFD to its statement on its FTC settlement: “Amazon and our executives have always followed the law and this settlement allows us to move forward and focus on innovating for customers.”

The FTC and Shutterstock did not respond to inquiries. The New York City Office of Technology and Innovation referred DFD to the mayor’s press office, which was not immediately available for comment.
Open-source EO isn’t off the table

A senior White House official on Tuesday declined to rule out additional executive action on open-source AI models — including those from China.

“There’s plenty of ongoing work in this space,” the official said in response to a question about whether the Trump administration plans to develop an open-source framework separate from President Donald Trump’s June 2 executive order on advanced AI.

The comments came during a call with reporters to discuss the rollout of a new AI cybersecurity clearinghouse known as Gold Eagle. But reporters also asked about escalating industry chatter that suggests the government is preparing to take action on open-source AI — models that let users access and sometimes tinker with the underlying architecture.

While open-source models are viewed as cheaper and more customizable than their closed-source counterparts, critics have raised safety and national security concerns about the technology. Top Chinese AI companies have favored open-source designs, adding to concerns among some national security hawks in Washington.

The White House official later dodged a separate question about whether the administration plans to take action that specifically targets Chinese open-source models, pivoting to praise America’s open-source AI ecosystem instead.

“I could not be more clear that we are in full support of the U.S. open-source community,” the official said.
X accedes to the EU

The European Commission announced Wednesday that X accepted its demands to adjust data access and transparency tools on the platform in order to comply with EU law, POLITICO’s Eliza Gkritsi reports.

The commission found in December that X violated the European Union’s Digital Services Act due to its deceptively designed blue checkmarks and failure to meet transparency obligations. The commission said in the announcement that X has committed to reforms like improving its ad repository’s speed and search functionality, and ensuring that researchers have free access to public data.

“The approved measures represent an important step in enabling researchers, civil society and the public in general to gain more transparency into X’s systems, in particular to monitor X’s systemic risks and to assess the platform’s broader impact on its users and European society as a whole,” the announcement reads.
