item.title: Apple’s OpenAI offensive
item.description: Apple’s OpenAI offensive
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Apple filed a major trade secrets lawsuit against OpenAI on Friday. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Apple filed a scorched-earth lawsuit on Friday accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets to launch a prospective line of consumer devices. The complaint alleges OpenAI gained confidential information from employees it poached from Apple. An OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement, “We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets. While we take these allegations seriously, we’re not aware of any evidence that this complaint has merit.” An Apple spokesperson told DFD, “Recently, significant evidence has emerged suggesting individuals employed by OpenAI wrongfully took Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products. We will always defend our teams' hard work and innovations[.]”

DFD spoke with Leander Kahney, editor of Cult of Mac — a long-running blog devoted to Apple news and commentary — about whether OpenAI poses a serious competitive threat to Apple and the potential ramifications of the lawsuit. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What stands out to you about this lawsuit?

The weird thing is that it's kind of like Keystone Cops industrial espionage. I was really surprised at how unsophisticated the alleged perpetrators were. Apple alleges that [the former employees] were emailing themselves confidential information using company devices, which just seems insane. A lot of the evidence seems to be pulled from personal messages that were sent to Apple devices or over Apple's network. I’d imagine Apple employees would've been employing Mission Impossible-type tactics to get this information out, but it seems relatively unsophisticated.

How much of a threat would OpenAI’s potential hardware business be to Apple?

That's a hard question to answer without knowing what [OpenAI] has got. But the first thing I thought when this lawsuit came out is that this is an effort to chill their hardware efforts. Nothing has come along in technology quite like AI in decades — it's the most fundamentally important technology since the dawn of personal computing itself. [Apple] must think that there's a very serious challenge going on with OpenAI.

Is there a particular line of Apple products that OpenAI could meaningfully challenge? 

If you look at the stories on what OpenAI is developing, it's a home companion device driven by voice. It might have a camera to see what's going on around you. It sounds like a HomePod with a camera, and maybe it's able to do some movement.

[OpenAI] is not going to take on the iPhone directly. Others have tried this, and it's completely unassailable. I think the opening, maybe, is a smart home device that knows everything about you. It sucks in all your emails, all your messages. It can recognize people, pets, different things that are happening in the household. AI is this glue that makes it super useful because it knows all these things about you, and so it becomes this new kind of home computer for the AI age.

How has Apple been faring in the AI boom? Is it at the forefront or does it risk falling behind?

They were definitely behind. Apple has not developed these enormous data center-driven frontier AI models that do incredible Nobel Prize-winning stuff like protein folding. They definitely didn't have anything as advanced as Claude or ChatGPT.

[But] you can see now that it wasn't about who could build the best data center model. It was about the practical application of AI. Siri AI has now shown that Apple is way ahead. The iPhone and Apple's whole ecosystem of devices is an enormous barrier for anybody else to get into this. People are not going to stop buying iPhones.

With Siri AI, it's going to become one of the primary ways that people interact with their devices. The fact that it's on their iPhones, in their devices, people aren’t going to choose another AI over Siri AI. It's going to become the default way that people interact with AI, and I think probably the most dominant AI for years to come because of that.

What could it mean if Apple wins the lawsuit?

They're looking for a judge to stop OpenAI from coming out with some of these devices — it's a very serious hurdle for OpenAI's hardware ambitions. It could completely upend their plans to come out with some hardware this next year if Apple gets a judge to grant the kind of preliminary injunction that it wants. For OpenAI, it's a serious problem — possibly existential for that company. They're running out of money so fast and they have this big IPO planned — it might put some serious doubts about that happening.

I'm sure a lot of other companies are also planning this kind of stuff for AI. There's a million and one startups and other companies that are looking at AI hardware, but they don't have the size, funding or impact that OpenAI does.

Meta has been pouring billions of dollars into AI, and it also has hardware ambitions. Google could come out with its own devices, Amazon too. I don't think [an Apple win] is going to have much of an effect on those other companies unless Apple launches more lawsuits.
Kevin O’Leary sued over data center claims

Two Utah nonprofits filed a defamation lawsuit against Kevin O’Leary and Fox News on Wednesday over the celebrity businessman's claims during appearances on the network concerning data centers, POLITICO’s Hassan Ali Kanu reports.

According to the complaint, O’Leary “without any evidence” accused opponents of his plan to build a 40,000-acre Utah data center of being “proxies for the Chinese government.” The suit alleges that O’Leary made those statements in at least 10 appearances on Fox News, and that the network kept inviting him back.

Fox News Media told POLITICO that it “publicly corrected the record on every program where on-air guest Kevin O’Leary’s comments were made, all of which was extensively publicized.” The network added that it “will vigorously defend against this lawsuit." O’Leary did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump sticks up for data centers too

President Donald Trump disparaged New York’s moratorium on data center construction in a Wednesday Truth Social post, POLITICO’s Nick Reisman reports.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order on Tuesday enacting the U.S.’s first state-level pause on data center construction for up to 12 months. “Governor Kathy Hochul, for political reasons, has terminated all Data Centers being built, or to be built, in New York State. These Companies are now being sought in Alabama, Florida, Texas, Arizona, and many other States,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Both the Taxes and the Jobs amount to LIQUID GOLD! New York State has made a terrible decision.”

Hochul replied in an X post: “If data centers are really ‘LIQUID GOLD,’ then New Yorkers deserve more than scraps. We hit pause because the communities powering AI should share in its success.”

item.title: 5 Questions for Stephanie T. Nguyen
item.description: 5 Questions for Stephanie T. Nguyen
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng

With help from Aaron Mak

Stephanie T. Nguyen | Handout.

Stephanie T. Nguyen was chief technologist at the Federal Trade Commission under President Joe Biden, where she led studies on artificial intelligence and surveillance pricing, and supported enforcement actions on competition and consumer protection. Nguyen is currently a senior fellow at Columbia Law School’s Center for Law and the Economy, where she is researching ways to help state and local regulators protect consumers and ensure fair competition. She talks to us about commercial surveillance’s effects on advertising and how lawmakers can use existing regulations to protect people from abuses in AI. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

We should be able to navigate a world without feeling like we are living in some endless game of Pac-Man, where the ghosts keep multiplying, there’s new threats at every turn, and the people who designed the game itself control the conditions, the incentives and the rules.

Elected officials, policymakers and regulators have the power now to aggressively enforce existing authorities and pass new legislation when needed and go after bad actors who break the laws.

But any attempts to address these problems that don’t fix these problems are missing the point. For example, adding more legalese into privacy policies as transparency doesn’t fix those problems. Sending people to consumer reporting mechanisms that don’t follow up or help them doesn’t fix those problems, or saying companies can just self-regulate and we can watch what happens in the next few years certainly won’t fix these problems either.

Can I go shopping and compare real prices? Can we not turn daycare or snacktime into surveillance? Can we live in your neighborhood in a place that doesn’t degrade your quality of life with basic resources?

I think an underrated big idea is to really put forth that North Star vision, and remember that the thing people want is to live their lives with quality.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

I would say advertising, marketing and the surveillance infrastructure around it.

Advertising and marketing is a massive infrastructure for collecting data, predicting behavior, targeting individuals, matching buyers to sellers, using AI to create all sorts of content, and optimize people’s engagement.

We’ve treated the ad economy as a normal part of life rather than a choice. It is now embedded into every single sector, which has become way more opaque, more widespread and more sophisticated to target individuals, not just with ads, but with prices too.

This has created a really strange convergence. Big retailers are effectively advertising companies now, they no longer just sell products. Big Tech companies are advertisers, they aren’t just social media companies connecting people. Advertisers are now Big Tech companies, they aren’t just promoting products, they’re building those ecosystems that are designed to capture, measure and monetize human behavior.

Advertising isn’t something anymore that companies do to sell more products, it’s the underlying infrastructure. It shapes how businesses operate, how markets function, how people experience everyday life.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

Two things: First is using existing laws more aggressively.

A big one is we need to close the commercial surveillance loophole. The need for high-quality training data isn’t going away, so we need to prohibit certain data from being collected, prohibit data sales and monetization or selling or sharing as default, and require data deletion.

There’s a strong body of FTC data broker cases that can serve as a good example for this.

As AI agents and AI chatbots begin to take shape in virtually every sector, prohibiting a platform with conflicts of interest such as self-preferencing. Should you be able to operate an AI agent if you operate a platform that connects consumers with marketplaces or if you have some financial interest in the outcome of product recommendations or if you earn revenue from ads?

The second thing is passing laws to help fill gaps without loopholes. I was chatting with my former Consumer Financial Protection Bureau colleagues about the idea to pass a law that says government auditors have ongoing supervisory authority — similar to bank supervisory authority — to examine companies’ algorithmic decision-making systems and pricing practices to ensure compliance with federal, state or local laws. Ideally, do these things before a crisis occurs, as opposed to after.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Here are two books that most recently have been on my mind.

The first one is because I have a tiny human in my house, and the book is Because a Little Bug Went Ka-Choo by Rosetta Stone, a.k.a. Dr. Seuss.

It’s a kids book about the chaos that unfolds after a tiny bug sneezes, so like a turtle gets bopped, a hen gets drenched, a farmer gets a bucket stuck on his head, and it all converges into this massive town parade.

It’s kind of this elegant distillation of cause and effect, and it captures the interconnectedness of the world and how a small action can create a long chain of unpredictable effects.

The second one is Crisis Engineering by friends and former colleagues of mine at U.S. Digital Service during the Obama administration. The book is about a useful way to think about how we work in and out of government. We are all cogs in the wheels of dozens of complex systems and within this, crisis can happen, which are significant changes in a short amount of time.

In thinking about the future generally, it’s less about predicting it and more about building the capacity to make sense of it quickly, and respond to it when it happens.

What has surprised you the most this year?

I often read a lot of articles or listen to podcasts, or hear panels in conversations that accept the premise that the cat’s out of the bag, or certain outcomes are inevitable.

We are told that we simply have to choose between the worst of the two evils. That we can get benefits of targeted surveillance discounts, or we can get no deals or no benefits at all. Or that we can have a world dominated by giant platforms with free convenient products that they provide or fall behind in global competition.

Policymakers, people often say, must balance innovation with regulations, as if these goals exist on opposite sides of a scale. But a competitive, fair and just market may be one of the strongest drivers of innovation.

So what has surprised me most is how quickly we have accepted these trade-offs that are built in today’s systems. These aren’t laws of nature, these are choices created by executives, and people who run businesses driven by incentives. If those are choices, they can be changed.
Democrats seek to influence chatbots

A progressive group that recruits candidates known as Run for Something has rolled out a new tool for campaigns to influence AI chatbot outputs, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp reports.

CampSight, which debuted last month, helps candidates examine what chatbots are saying about them to users. The tool also analyzes chatbot citations to offer pointers on how candidates can induce more favorable responses — with interventions such as rewording their campaign website’s issues page or submitting a Ballotpedia candidate profile. (Ballotpedia CEO and founder Leslie Graves told POLITICO that the site retains editorial discretion over profiles.)

A couple dozen campaigns are now using CampSight, and about 350 candidates and advocacy groups are on the waitlist, according to Run for Something Executive Director Amanda Litman. “We know that the most scientifically proven way to get someone to vote is to have a personal relationship with a candidate,” said Litman. “Everything else in a campaign is about replicating that intimacy between voter and candidate. This is just another way of doing that.”
Poll shows growing data center opposition

New findings from The POLITICO Poll indicate that disapproval of datacenters has risen sharply over the first half of the year, POLITICO’s Katherine Long and Jessie Blaeser report.

A July survey of 2,061 respondents by the independent polling organization Public First indicates that 41 percent of Americans would oppose the construction of a data center within three miles of where they live, up from 28 percent in a January POLITICO Poll. There was also a drop in support for data centers from 37 percent to 24 percent in that six-month period.

The negative shift in opinion was present on the right and left, though it was particularly pronounced among respondents who said they’d voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. “It's rare to see political attitudes change this fast in an era where they are often quite static and partisan,” said Public First head of polling Seb Wride.

item.title: How AI will fragment the internet
item.description: How AI will fragment the internet
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Hassan Ali Kanu

AI chatbots have to navigate a maze of speech laws abroad. | Martin Lelievre/AFP via Getty Images

The technolibertarian dream of a borderless internet may soon get its biggest reality check in years.

Meta’s Oversight Board — a governance body launched in 2020 that continues to independently make binding content moderation decisions and policy recommendations — released a report last week suggesting that large language models could be “stifling political speech.” A study of 10 commercial LLMs found that the models may be essentially censoring themselves based on the speech laws of countries around the world.

What the board seems to find more concerning, however, is that the AI chatbots appear at times to be applying one country’s more repressive speech restrictions globally. For instance, multiple chatbots refused to create flyers critical of Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman or China’s President Xi Jinping. Yet they would do so for U.S. President Donald Trump and U.K. King Charles III.

The report recommends that AI companies emulate social media platforms and ensure one censorship regime doesn’t affect how LLMs function in other countries. Social networks have spent two decades Balkanizing their moderation policies to achieve this balance. It’s hard to see how AI doesn’t follow suit.

“The idea that we would get one global standard that was aspired to by social media companies was never going to be where we ended up,” said Heidi J.S. Tworek, director of the University of British Columbia’s Centre for the Study of Democratic Institutions. “I don't see why that's going to be different for LLMs … It's very difficult to imagine a world where for the first time we have one global standard of freedom of expression.”

Despite bold proclamations of free speech absolutism, social media companies have struggled to navigate draconian limitations on political expression in certain countries. Facebook previously blocked groups critical of the monarchy in Thailand, and Iran and China have banned various social networks. Platforms have also grappled with speech rules in liberal democracies. Germany, for example, prohibits the dissemination of Nazi and Holocaust-denial content online.

Due to the variation in speech laws, the only way to have one global content standard for social media or LLMs would be to play by the strictest rules. “At the end of the day, you have two options,” Dalhousie University tech and law professor Michael Karanicolas told DFD. “You can either have everybody censored to Saudi/Chinese/Russian [rules], or you can carve off those particular jurisdictions.”

The Oversight Board’s report suggests fragmenting AI content rules may be the best option, suggesting that chatbots could operate similarly to social media by “geo-blocking content in specific jurisdictions in compliance with applicable law, while ensuring that it remains available to users elsewhere.” The board did not respond to an inquiry.

Yet there are key differences between AI and traditional social media platforms that could make it difficult to tailor chatbot content based on local laws.

“What strikes me with these large language models is there's already so much confusion and unpredictability about the results that they're returning as it is,” said Karanicolas. “The idea of then geolocating and trying to get different results for different people in different jurisdictions — it doesn't surprise me that that's extremely difficult given the challenge that these companies have faced in filtering out things like defamatory content.”

Unlike social media, which functions more as a town square, chatbots are private conversational partners whose responses are directed at individual users. That makes it harder for governments to monitor LLM interactions and enforce speech restrictions. The challenge is compounded when users devise ways around those rules. China, for example, has spent years suppressing references to Winnie the Pooh, after social media users began invoking the cartoon bear as code for President Xi. Detecting similar attempts to circumvent a chatbot’s political guardrails will be far more difficult in one-on-one conversations.

“Obviously there were many attempts to manipulate social media, but the way in which you can try and manipulate LLMs is somewhat different,” Tworek told DFD. “[There are] a whole host of differences in the more private nature of the chat and the potential ability for users to jailbreak it a little bit as well.”
Meta may dodge $1.4 trillion fine

Meta appears unlikely to be hit with a record-setting trillion-dollar penalty if it loses a consumer protection lawsuit brought by 29 states.

U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers characterized the states’ proposed penalties that reach up to $1.4 trillion as “staggering” and potential “overreach,” while adding that Meta’s counterproposal of $4 million is “not even a slap on the hand” for a business of its size.

The trial is scheduled to start next month, and is one of thousands of cases consolidated into multi-district litigation seeking to hold Meta and other social media companies responsible for alleged harms caused by their platforms, including that the apps are addictive by design.

“You both have taken positions in this case that are in the extremes,” Gonzalez Rogers told attorneys for both sides during a hearing on Friday.

The states’ attorneys signaled they may drop the trillion-dollar request, saying they submitted “potential” and “legally permissible” penalty options with the understanding that a judge or jury would weigh in with separate considerations. That means penalties could still reach into the hundreds of millions of dollars.

The states’ penalty proposals were calculated based on legal fine amounts and the estimated numbers of individual teens and individual instances of violations. A New Mexico jury hit Meta with $375 million in penalties in March in a separate case that involved similar allegations, and a judge in the state is currently considering additional, non-monetary relief.

Meta is also facing a similar lawsuit brought by Tennessee. A trial and jury selection in that case kicked off today.
Top AI safety official departs

Center for AI Standards and Innovation Director Chris Fall has resigned after only three months in the role, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp and Sophia Cai report.

Fall has been central to the Trump administration’s efforts to vet frontier models submitted voluntarily by developers prior to public release. CAISI announced deals with Microsoft, xAI and Google DeepMind in May to evaluate their models for national security risks.

“Following Chris’s departure, NIST Director Dr. Arvind Raman will continue to oversee CAISI and will serve as Acting CAISI Director,” said a Commerce Department spokesperson. An official at the department, granted anonymity to discuss personnel issues, said that Raman will spearhead the search for a replacement who will be announced in the coming weeks. The official also indicated that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is keen to find someone with AI expertise. Axios previously reported details of Fall’s resignation.

item.title: China’s grand AI showcase
item.description: China’s grand AI showcase
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks at the opening ceremony for the World AI Conference on July 17 in Shanghai. | Ng Han Guan-Pool/Getty Images

Chinese President Xi Jinping laid out a comprehensive vision for global AI regulation in his keynote address during his first appearance at the annual World Artificial Intelligence Conference, which was held over the weekend. Xi pressed for an open-source AI ecosystem and international collaboration to integrate the technology in the Global South. He also warned that no one country should determine the course of AI development — which some commentators interpreted as a swipe at America’s dominance in the field. 

DFD spoke to Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies senior fellow Samm Sacks — who attended WAIC to engage in informal diplomatic talks between civil society organizations — for an on-the-ground perspective. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

A lot of news coverage has interpreted Xi’s keynote as challenging American AI dominance. Did you get that sense?

There's this temptation to read geopolitics and competition with the U.S. into everything the Chinese leadership does. It's certainly a really important driver, but so much of what is happening in Beijing oftentimes has nothing to do with the United States and is also very much about domestic pressures.

So some of this is China saying: "We're here on the world stage. We're a peer competitor of the U.S.” On the other hand, we have to also forget the U.S. for a moment and recognize that there are very powerful domestic factors at play, which make Xi's stamp of authority on AI initiatives and investment also about delivering goods to the public in terms of economic growth.

What was the sentiment at WAIC around Kimi K3, a model unveiled by the Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI on Friday, and how it purportedly rivals the U.S.’s top AI tech?

It was fascinating to be on the ground in Shanghai with this confluence of events. You have Xi Jinping keynoting WAIC for the first time. You have Moonshot AI unveiling its incredibly powerful new model, Kimi K3. I don't think that's a coincidence. It’s not to say that the labs are controlled by the government — they're not. But the timing was very much, from my view, coordinated to showcase that China is, if not at the frontier, certainly a strong rival.

I visited the Kimi booth at the exhibition hall. What I was told when I spoke with some of the people there is that this is the next DeepSeek moment. This flies in the face of a purported U.S. strategy to curb China's advancements by restricting access to compute.

What did you gather from your diplomatic dialogues at WAIC, and did it tell you anything about the feasibility of the U.S. and China agreeing on AI ground rules?

There was just this level of hunger for substantive conversation. There's a lot at stake when you talk about a Mythos-level cyber capability, and that's something that's really scary for all sides. And it's not just cybersecurity. There was a lot of discussion about a news report that talked about Boko Haram having a dedicated AI team that they were using for weapons.

Some issues that were floated in [diplomatic dialogues] were things like AI incident reporting. If an AI system goes astray and there's harm that's experienced, is there a mechanism that both sides can use to share that information? There's this recognition that we can't face these things alone.

One caveat is that I think in China, there's a recognition that Trump is erratic and unpredictable. As much as we may want this kind of stability and rational conversation around risk, we're dealing with the reality of a president that has wild swings — we have to price that in too. That was, from my perception, very much part of the conversation too.

What do you think is WAIC’s significance in terms of soft power and China’s influence over the global AI ecosystem? 

There were many countries [from the Global South] that came to the conference for Xi Jinping’s speech that buy into this idea of Chinese leadership pushing out open-weight AI as a public good. But there's an open question too about how much of that is a demand signal. It may also be that there's a strong demand in countries in the Global South for affordable open AI models that can be used to turbocharge their own digital economies.

The U.S. government came out and essentially prohibited foreign nationals from using advanced models [i.e. Anthropic’s Fable 5]. It set off this chain reaction around the world where a lot of governments were like: "The U.S. can, on a whim, deny access to foreign nationals to these AI models. Why would we go with them when we can go with a Chinese model that nobody has a kill switch on? "
New Jersey restricts rent algorithms

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a bill Monday that prohibits the use of algorithms to coordinate rental prices, POLITICO’s Joey Fox reports.

The Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent Act is designed to prevent landlords from colluding to artificially inflate housing costs with the help of AI. New York, Connecticut and California have previously enacted similar legislation. POLITICO’s Nate Robson previously reported for DFD on how regulators are increasingly concerned that algorithms could be used — whether intentionally or incidentally — to gouge consumers.

“The problem is that these tools put competing landlords on the same team against renters,” Sherrill, a Democrat, said at the bill signing ceremony. “Landlords can use these algorithms to coordinate prices, move in lockstep, and push rents higher and higher. It’s collusion by algorithm, it’s illegal, and it stacks the deck against renters.”

The FAIR Act aligns with Sherrill’s agenda on affordability and regulating the tech sector, though it has drawn opposition from some industry groups and Republican legislators. “Truth be told, if you address algorithms, it’s not really going to materially change the rent prices in this state. We have underlying structural issues,” said New Jersey Builders Association CEO Jeff Kolakowski at a committee hearing last month. Proponents of the bill like 32BJ SEIU argue that it will still help lower costs. “The housing crisis wasn’t created by algorithms, but algorithms are contributing to it,” said Ana Maria Hill, the union’s state director.
Florida governor race hones in on data centers

Opposition to data centers is becoming an increasingly common talking point in Florida’s gubernatorial election, POLITICO’s Kylie Williams reports.

Democratic front-runner David Jolly reiterated his support for a statewide data center moratorium in a video posted to X on Tuesday, in which he accused leading Republican candidate Rep. Byron Donalds of wanting to “hand pristine Florida land over to the industry funding his campaign.” Jolly advocated for a moratorium last week as well.

Donalds campaign spokesperson Gates McGavick responded in a statement that “Byron Donalds has made it clear he supports protecting Florida ratepayers and communities.” McGavick added, “No ratepayer and environmental protections, no data centers. Period.” Nearly every candidate in the race has voiced a position on regulating data centers.

As Kylie also reported, the Donalds campaign has received millions of dollars from AI groups and companies that are aiming to build hyperscale data centers in Florida. In response, the campaign emphasized Donalds’ introduction of the Protecting Ratepayers Act in the House on Monday “to ensure that private developers, rather than American taxpayers, bear the investment costs of data center developments that advance our country's technological dominance.”

item.title: What happens if data-driven pricing gets it wrong
item.description: What happens if data-driven pricing gets it wrong
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng

With help from Aaron Mak

A study found that Home Depot's algorithms often make wrong inferences about customers. | Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Using the data it collected on its customer — a man in a household of four — Home Depot’s algorithms inferred he was a European woman living in a home with six other people.

Another customer, a college student with one roommate, was assumed to be a middle-aged renter with children.

As more businesses explore using artificial intelligence to set personalized prices for customers — a practice referred to as “surveillance pricing” or “data-driven pricing” — a new report from academics studying tech policy questions the accuracy of such data collections.

Flights, groceries and rideshare prices set by algorithms have raised concerns among lawmakers, who worry that people’s data will be used to raise prices, leading to laws in New Jersey, Maryland, Connecticut and New York to outlaw the practice.

Industry groups have pushed back against regulations, arguing that businesses use people’s data to offer personalized discounts and target lower prices to attract customers.

Data has been crucial to retail strategy for over a decade, with chains such as Walmart and Kroger creating detailed profiles of their customers. A 2023 paper from NetChoice, which represents companies such as Amazon, Google and Meta, said the profiles would help provide lower prices and improved shopping experiences.

These inference-based customer profiles are only expected to expand with AI, said Eric Null, Center for Democracy and Technology’s Privacy & Data Project director, at a panel about inference-based data practices on Tuesday.

“AI can easily categorize people based on behavioral data, and then companies can build advertising ecosystems based off of those inferences,” Null said.

The report from New York University, Columbia University and Northeastern University researchers shows that such customer profiles can be riddled with errors.

The study had 10 participants send data access requests to Home Depot, which the researchers focused on because of the company’s large data collection through its in-house advertising company Orange Apron Media and investments in artificial intelligence to improve sales.

It found errors in customers’ profiles, including wrong inferences about people’s jobs, gender, ages and how many kids they had, according to the report.

Stephanie Nguyen, a former chief technologist at the Federal Trade Commission and a co-author of the research paper, told Digital Future Daily the errors could cascade if they are shared with other companies.

“That profile gets sold or shared to other companies. Then it's used to decide what they pay, or whether they get the deal — or the opportunity at all — based on inferences that can be wrong,” she said.

Home Depot spokesperson Beth Marlowe said the company doesn’t use inferences to provide its customers with discounts, and that customers can submit requests to correct their information or opt out of having it shared.

But customers are unlikely to know their profiles have the wrong information to begin with, Nguyen explained.

“Consumers don’t get a fair shake, no way to challenge the price they’re given, and often no idea it ever happened,” she said.
OpenAI models escape containment

OpenAI disclosed on Tuesday that its AI models broke loose onto the open internet and executed a fully autonomous cyberattack last week, POLITICO’s John Sakellariadis and Dana Nickel report.

OpenAI said in a blog post that a combination of its models, including the company’s new GPT‑5.6 Sol and an even more powerful unreleased model, hacked parts of the AI platform Hugging Face after escaping during internal testing. Hugging Face announced that its own open-weight AI was able to detect and thwart the breach.

The events appear to constitute one of the first known cases of AI performing a multi-step cyberattack by itself, rather than aiding a human hacker. OpenAI is working with Hugging Face to investigate the incident, and is implementing new guardrails for its testing processes. “We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly,” OpenAI said.
Microsoft commits $60M to Genesis Mission

Microsoft unveiled a $60 million investment package on Wednesday in support of the Energy Department’s Genesis Mission to accelerate scientific research with AI, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp reports.

The investment is one of the largest contributions to the Genesis Mission, which President Donald Trump launched in November with an executive order. Microsoft has committed to contributing $40 million in Azure compute and AI credits, and $20 million in engineering and technical support services. The company’s new Scientific Partnership Advancing Research & Knowledge coordination hub will facilitate its work with the Genesis Mission.

“Through the Genesis Mission, Microsoft is committing to work as part of America’s research enterprise by providing hyperscale compute, advanced models, emerging quantum capabilities and dedicated expertise that run alongside the labs’ own world-leading systems,” Chris Barry, president of Microsoft’s U.S. Public Sector Industries, said in a statement.

item.title: When AI breaks containment
item.description: When AI breaks containment
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Owen Dahlkamp

OpenAI's models autonomously launched a cyberattack after escaping onto the open internet. | Michael Dwyer/AP

OpenAI disclosed this week that a combination of its models launched a fully autonomous cyberattack against the AI platform Hugging Face after escaping a secure testing environment during a benchmarking evaluation. Hugging Face pointed DFD to a blog post indicating its systems prevented the breach. OpenAI did not respond to an inquiry, but it has committed to working with Hugging Face to investigate the incident. This appears to be one of the first known cases of AI performing a multi-step cyberattack by itself. To understand the implications of the incident, DFD spoke with Semgrep co-founder and CTO Drew Dennison — whose cybersecurity firm has conducted risk evaluations of OpenAI’s most advanced models prior to release as part of the company’s Trusted Access for Cyber program. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

You’ve been able to test OpenAI’s most advanced models prior to release as part of its Trusted Access for Cyber program. Did you find this incident surprising, or was it to be expected?

This incident wasn't surprising to me. This matches my level of exposure with Mythos, which we had early access to, as well as OpenAI's trusted cyber program. What that's enabled us to do is really see the models with mostly removed cyber guardrails. The models are extremely capable of finding bugs and exploiting them to reach their goal.

I was a little surprised that OpenAI's sandboxing environment [a secure testing environment that restricts models’ internet access] wasn't stronger, but it was only a matter of time. This is going to be the new normal going forward where every service will be subjected to hundreds of AI agents constantly trying to break in.

How will the cybersecurity industry need to adjust if there are an increasing number of attacks that don’t involve a human hacker?

The main thing is the defensive hardening of our code bases. For far too long, people have kind of [thought], “We'll get to security when we can.” The average time to patch is still in the hundreds of days for a lot of services. We got around it because there are only so many attackers in the world, and they only had so much time. So if you weren't in the crosshairs, you were probably okay. Now we just have to live in a world where everything is constantly being probed.

Human [hackers] get bored, and move on to other tasks. The model doesn't care. It's just going to continually try to go for whatever goal has been set.

Open-source models are quickly advancing toward having the same capabilities of OpenAI’s tech, and there aren’t sandbox protections around them. What will keep motivating companies to keep sandboxing, given that they aren’t required to do so?

We still want to try to avoid harm. Organizations that are following laws and norms should still run everything inside of a sandbox. We certainly do.

You could imagine corporate liability. That didn't happen in this case — OpenAI and Hugging Face are holding hands on this. But if models came out of Semgrep’s lab, we could certainly be liable for any harm it caused.

Some lawmakers have responded to the incident by calling for mandatory government security testing of frontier models prior to release. Do you think that’s warranted given this latest cyberattack?

No, and actually I think it's harmful. [When] the defenders didn't have access to the best models to investigate what was going on, it harmed the people who were trying to protect software. And if we zoom outside this lab context, we need every firm to have help protecting their software. If we slow that down with delays, that harms [those efforts].

If it was only two firms in the world that had this technology, then regulatory answers could make sense. But because we're seeing that the open-weight models are catching up rapidly … I think it's going to be impossible to regulate it.

Other lawmakers say it should be mandatory to report these incidents to the Commerce Department and its Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Are those kinds of requirements warranted?

I am in favor of more transparency and reporting. As an industry, we've [been] too hush-hush. Maybe someone got hacked, but they don't want to have to talk about it. Sunlight is the best disinfectant here. Industry bodies need to start sharing best practices with each other. These are not competitive things. We as an industry need to collaborate.
Grassley wants answers on Meta whistleblowers

Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) is asking Meta to respond to allegations it fired two employees who he said were serving as whistleblowers to his committee.

The two whistleblowers — Joshua DeFriez and William Sevedge — were fired from Meta after providing information and documents to the committee about Meta’s “disregard for child safety risks,” their lawyers wrote to Grassley and committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) on July 1.

DeFriez and Sevedge provided information for a September subcommittee hearing titled “Hidden Harms: Examining Whistleblower Allegations that Meta Buried Child Safety Research,” but opted to remain anonymous, Grassley wrote in a letter to Meta executives Wednesday. The duo decided to disclose their names publicly after facing alleged retaliation.

In the letter, Grassley questioned Meta about its policies regarding whistleblowers, whether Meta surveils employees in an attempt to identify “leakers” and the accuracy of DeFriez and Sevedge’s allegations. He asked for a response by Aug. 5.

“These individuals were laid off due to business reasons and during separate large-scale reductions in force,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said in a statement. “We had no awareness they were in touch with the committee until we heard from their lawyers after the layoffs had taken place."
Macron wins big with a social media ban

France’s social media ban is a major victory for President Emmanuel Macron and his tech legacy, POLITICO’s Klara Durand and Océane Herrero report.

France's parliament approved a law on Tuesday that prohibits kids under the age of 15 from using social media, making it the first country in the European Union to introduce such a ban.

Throughout his presidency, episodes of unrest — from the 2018 nationwide Yellow Jackets protests to the riots that followed the police shooting of teenager Nahel Merzouk in 2023 — reinforced Macron's conviction that social media had fueled polarization.

The issue became personal when the president and his family were targeted by repeated online attacks, including false rumors about his marriage and cyberbullying directed at first lady Brigitte Macron. Platforms will be required to implement age verification measures starting on Sept. 1.

“I had promised to do this, and it has now been passed: social media will be banned for under-15s when the new school year begins,” Macron wrote on X.

item.title: Harsh penalties for data brokers in New Jersey threaten campaign tech
item.description: Harsh penalties for data brokers in New Jersey threaten campaign tech
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng and Daniel Han

With help from Aaron Mak

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherill signed a law to crack down on data brokers in June. | Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images

New Jersey looked to crack down on data brokers by passing a strict new law to prevent the sale of personal data. Instead, it's causing chaos over the last month for the state’s electoral system.

A new bill, A-5328, was signed into law by Gov. Mikie Sherill (D) just 48 hours after it was introduced during the Legislature’s rush to pass the state budget. The measure has since rattled the political tech world.

Campaign consultants, advertisers, Democrats and Republicans have warned that the law could sweep in political data firms, raising the prospect of steep registration fees and potentially massive fines for handling voter data.

The concern stems from its creation of the nation’s most expensive data broker registry, along with the broadest definition yet of who can be held liable for penalties.

Those provisions could impose significant costs and risks for campaigns and companies that collect and share voter data, with annual registration fees ranging from $5,000 to $1.5 million, depending on how much data they acquire. States with similar registries, including Texas and California, charge $300 and $6,000, respectively.

Violators also face penalties of up to $50,000 per record for unlawfully selling data, including demographic information such as race, religious beliefs and location.

“Few campaigns, political parties, or civic organizations on either side of the aisle will be able to risk using voter data to communicate with New Jerseyans, which means less door knocking, less voter contact, and less accurate information reaching the people who need it before an election,” Mark Jablonowski, the president of the Democratic digital advertising firm DSPolitical, said.

The American Association of Political Consultants, a nonpartisan political consulting trade group, called for the law to be repealed, arguing it will limit national and state campaigns’ ability to reach voters in New Jersey.

Sherrill and the Democratic-led Legislature are both looking at revisiting the bill’s language following backlash against the law that’s only been on the books for less than a month. The Sherrill administration has said that enforcement guidance will be unveiled in the coming months.

A spokesperson for New Jersey Assembly Democrats told POLITICO that the bill was not intended to limit political speech or create barriers to run for office.

“We are aware that the Sherrill Administration is conducting a review of the law, we are conducting one as well,” spokesperson Rhonda Schaffler said in a statement. “If it becomes necessary to make clear that a law regulating data brokers does not limit the First Amendment or harm political communication, we will review and consider options together with the Senate and the Governor.”

The issue has turned into a political opportunity for state Republicans, who have criticized Democrats for rushing the law through. They have expressed concerns about the law banning the sale of location data, which campaigns use to target ads to voters in relevant districts.

“It really has created the situation where candidates and campaigns are nervous about proceeding and how does this affect them with no guidance and no carveout,” New Jersey GOP Chair Christine Hanlon told POLITICO. “It really is a problem that needs to be addressed.”

Hanlon added that litigation over the new law was “not out of the question.”
Big Tech backs open-weight models

More than 20 major tech companies called on the Trump administration to ensure that open-weight AI models remain widely available in a Friday open letter, which was first shared with POLITICO’s Katherine Long.

The administration is currently considering a ban on open-weight models from China due to national security concerns. The letter — whose signatories include A16z, Dell, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia and Palantir — contends that access to open-weight models enables competition that “keeps the gains of AI broadly shared rather than concentrated in a few hands.”

“By allowing many organizations to build, adapt, and deploy advanced models, open weights create rivalry not only among model developers but across cloud chips, applications, and services,” the letter reads. “That competition spurs innovation, drives down costs, and distributes the benefits of AI broadly across our economy.”

White House discussions of a potential ban were rekindled after the Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI unveiled its advanced open-weight Kimi K3 model last week. The companies acknowledged that open-weight models pose distinct risks around cybersecurity and misuse, but that such concerns “should be addressed through targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions on techniques that play an important role in AI innovation.”
EU accuses TikTok of privacy failures

The European Commission accused TikTok of violating online platform regulations by allegedly failing to adequately safeguard minors’ privacy, POLITICO’s Eliza Gkritsi reports.

Commission officials released preliminary findings of an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with safety standards in the European Union’s Digital Service Act on Friday. The officials said that minors’ accounts on TikTok are too easily discoverable, and that the platform’s privacy settings do not sufficiently protect young users from predatory behavior or unwanted contact.

TikTok spokesperson Mireia Quingles told POLITICO that “under 18 accounts are private by default and we are one of the only platforms where younger teens cannot use direct messaging or have their content eligible to appear in the ‘For You’ feed.” She added that the company “will review these preliminary findings.”

item.title: Inside the AI industry’s political war room
item.description: Inside the AI industry’s political war room
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Calder McHugh

With help from Chase DiFeliciantonio and Aaron Mak

Leading the Future is pouring millions of dollars into the midterm elections. | Sean Rayford/Getty Images

You may not have heard their names before. But two old school political operatives are steering the artificial intelligence industry’s biggest pot of political cash heading into the midterms.

Josh Vlasto, a Democrat, and Zac Moffatt, a Republican, are the co-heads of Leading the Future, a network of pro-AI industry super PACs and nonprofits that friends and foes describe as an aggressive, well-funded machine focused on obliterating opponents.

Their goal: to defeat candidates who support the strictest AI regulations and champion those who want to unleash the development of the industry. The PAC launched with over $100 million in the bank from some of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, including $25 million checks from a16z’s co-founder Marc Andreessen and OpenAI’s president Greg Brockman.

How they spend that mountain of money in the coming months will have a profound effect on the country’s political trajectory — and determine how lawmakers grapple with a technology that has the potential to transform society and our way of life.

Their record so far is formidable.

Leading the Future’s political arms — American Mission, which has operated in Republican primaries, and Think Big, which has operated in Democratic ones — have sent money to 30 candidates, and only one of their picks has lost so far. They’ve spent almost $25 million and still have over $30 million in cash on hand, according to an FEC filing through June 30. Their latest primary victories came Tuesday, when their preferred candidates won House GOP and Democratic primary races in Arizona.

Their strategy appears to include both carrots and sticks. Sometimes they wade into races with modest sums of money in a bid to build a bench of friendly lawmakers; but they’ve also signaled that they’ve got a bazooka ready to deploy against adversaries where needed.

Yet to hear Moffatt and Vlasto tell it, they’re actually the little guy.

“We get pointed to in a certain way — that it’s David vs. Goliath,” Moffatt said “I would argue we’re the David in this situation.”

That’s because, according to Moffatt and Vlasto, they are up against a diffuse universe of nonprofits, political action committees, media outlets, lobbyists and other tech executives — a faction they spitefully referred to as “doomers.” Many are associated with effective altruism and the “AI safety” movement that is an influential part of Silicon Valley.

So far, LTF has courted controversy, most notably in the Democratic primary in NY-12, where they spent over $8 million to successfully defeat the AI Safety-associated Alex Bores. Some of their hardnosed tactics, though, including building a network of meme “sockpuppet” accounts, have many in the industry and associated with AI politics looking askance at the group.

In June, OpenAI released a statement distancing itself from LTF, saying, “Groups that are advocating on AI should be clear about their policy views, be honest about whom they represent, and not use tactics like astroturfing that obscure the real choices facing policymakers and the public.”

But the Bores primary is far from the end of the LTF story. 

“The amount of money they’ve raised and the amount they spent on Bores was a warning shot for 2028,” said one AI and politics insider who was granted anonymity to discuss internal dynamics at Leading the Future. “They didn’t create this infrastructure just to influence the 2026 midterms.”

It is one of the most intoxicating environments for a couple of political veterans who don’t mind a little bit of risk: a giant issue, growing in salience, with its political contours not yet defined. Vlasto and Moffatt have been accused of many things. What you can’t call them is afraid of the fight.

Their checkbook is large, their ambitions are titanic and their work is still beginning. They want nothing less than to change America’s future and shape the country’s most prominent politicians’ views on the development of one of the world’s most consequential technologies.

“This is the first inning of many,” said Moffatt. “November is a stop on the journey. It’s part of a larger destination.”

Read the full profile of Vlasto, Moffatt and Leading the Future in POLITICO Magazine.
Hugging Face hack raises disclosure questions

The Hugging Face hack that OpenAI disclosed last week may have seemed like the first major test for California’s landmark AI transparency law that Gov. Gavin Newsom signed last year.

Except under that law, OpenAI wasn’t required to tell the state anything, our colleague Chase DiFeliciantonio reports from San Francisco in in today’s California Decoded newsletter.

Prior amended-away versions of the legislation (SB 53) would have covered this kind of cyberattack, but without a program causing certain major damage or bodily injury, companies can stay mum. OpenAI, of course, still did go public with the incident that happened during testing.

Lawmakers in Washington are now pushing for reporting requirements, and for some programs to have a so-called “kill switch” should they go rogue, but California lawmakers have been less strident in their calls for change.

The kill switch idea was contemplated in SB 1047, the first attempt at major AI regulation by California state Sen. Scott Wiener, which Newsom vetoed.

Neither Wiener nor Newsom, both looking to national political offices, are presently advocating for a big red OFF button on rogue AI programs. But an earlier version of SB 53, Wiener’s bill that Newsom signed last year, would have also made OpenAI’s loss of control over its program something that had to be reported to the state.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office is tasked with bringing civil actions under the law and handling AI whistleblower complaints.

In a recent interview with POLITICO’s Dasha Burns, Bonta insisted AI wasn’t an unregulated space, pushing back on Burns’ comparison of the AI regulation space to the “Wild West.”

“We have the ability to enforce all the laws, including the new laws that have been passed,” Bonta told Burns when asked specifically about the recent cybersecurity incident. “California has new laws that provide strong regulatory oversight.”
U.S. recruits 6G allies

The Trump administration is launching a global partnership Monday with more than 20 allied countries for secure 6G wireless network development , POLITICO’s John Hendel was the first to report.

Countries such as the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan are joining the initiative, which will set up points of contact across partnering governments, facilitate technical resource sharing and lay the foundation for commercial 6G deployment. The partnership is aimed at countering China’s telecom ambitions and the global influence of companies like Huawei and ZTE.

“We must take concrete steps to strengthen our 6G supply chains, accelerate innovation, and ensure that the future of wireless communications is shaped by like-minded nations,” the initiative’s call to action reads.

item.title: Prediction markets face a clash with state election laws
item.description: Prediction markets face a clash with state election laws
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

State bans on election betting could be an obstacle for prediction markets like Polymarket. | Théo Marie-Courtois/AFP via Getty Images

State laws on election betting could be a problem for prediction markets, particularly with the approaching midterms in the fall.

As the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports, Wisconsin regulators have warned residents over the past month that they could run afoul of an 1849 state law by placing prediction market bets on elections in which they later vote. A recent Pew Research study found that 23 states have laws like Wisconsin’s banning betting on elections, while another nine states impose narrower restrictions on the practice.

Yet many of these laws were enacted before modern online prediction markets were established, and they’ve rarely been enforced. As prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket skyrocket in popularity, and joust with local regulators, election betting could soon become the subject of a power struggle between states and the federal government.

“With sports, you could argue it's just a game,” said Jason Kido Lopez, a University of Wisconsin-Madison communications professor who studies betting. “The seriousness gets a lot more ramped up, some think, around election betting.”

Betting on elections was very popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries. It used to be common for newspapers to cite the odds in reporting on the state of a race before the advent of modern political polling.

Many of the state bans on election betting were enacted in that period, driven by concerns that such wagers would lead to electoral fraud and a corruption of democracy. Yet the bans often weren’t enforced, according to University of Michigan economic history professor Paul Rhode, due in part to concerns about disenfranchising voters.

Those bans were occasionally enforced in cases where prominent figures publicly boasted about their election bets. August Belmont, a 19th-Century Democratic National Committee chair, had his vote challenged after he publicly touted a wager against President Abraham Lincoln’s reelection.

“These cases were where people got way out there with their statements and their use of bets,” Rhode told DFD. “They were prominent people, so somebody might call them to account.” Regulators feared that a famous figure putting a lot of money down on an election outcome could unduly influence other voters.

Similar concerns about warping the democratic process seem to be animating the recent interest in state election betting regulations. Wisconsin election officials have expressed fears that the activity will motivate voters to pick candidates based on potential payouts, rather than merit.

Election prediction markets could also create incentives for candidates in lower-profile races to deliberately throw elections, echoing concerns that have long surrounded sports betting, according to Baruch College gaming law professor Marc Edelman. “The establishment of prediction markets on elections with real financial consequences for the bettors creates a very minimal value to society, with the possibility of greater negative externalities [in terms of] the potential, at least in lower level elections, for there to be intentional sabotage to win bets for others,” he told DFD.

It may also be easier for wealthier bettors to manipulate prediction market forecasts in lower-profile elections, which could influence voters who are consulting the odds to get a sense for who’s winning. “The volume of people putting money on some of these smaller races is not very large,” said DePaul University business law associate professor Karl Lockhart. “So if you have millions of dollars, you could … make it look like one side is sizably in the lead, and that could discourage voters from coming to vote, because they think the election is already in one side's hands rather than the other.”

However, conflicts between the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and states over prediction market regulations represent a potential obstacle for enforcement of state election betting laws.

The CFTC has recently tried to argue in court that it has the sole authority to regulate online prediction market platforms. According to the agency, prediction markets facilitate commodities investing rather than gambling, arguably putting them within the exclusive ambit of CFTC regulation.

Yet regulations around commodities investing recognize that there’s a societal benefit to being able to hedge against potential events like a decline in crop prices — which can allow farmers to remain financially stable. It’s less clear if it’s as important to be able to hedge against election results, Lockhart told DFD.

“The question I think we need to return to is [whether] there’s some sort of social benefit to allow people to bet on elections,” he said. “If that social benefit is there, is it bigger than the costs … [of] potential election manipulation?”

“As courts have recognized, prediction markets on CFTC-registered exchanges are governed by federal law, not a patchwork of state rules,” a Polymarket spokesperson told DFD in a statement.

The CFTC and Kalshi did not respond to inquiries.
Pornhub rebukes lawmakers

Pornhub sent a fiery letter on Tuesday to more than 300 lawmakers, governors and attorneys general, accusing them of jeopardizing privacy and safety by backing online age verification laws.

The adult content company argued in the letter, which was first obtained by POLITICO, that online age verification laws are detrimental to privacy because they require hundreds of thousands of websites to collect personal information from every user who wants to access adult content. The company also pointed to evidence from UK regulators suggesting that enforcing the country's Online Safety Act has pushed users to noncompliant sites. Pornhub urges the officials to instead institute device-based age verification policies.

“[W]e are deeply concerned about the harm being caused by the performative, ineffective, and unenforceable age verification laws you have taken part in passing despite your intention of protecting minors,” Pornhub wrote. The missive was addressed to prominent age verification advocates including Republican Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Democratic Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
xAI sues Minnesota over deepfakes

Elon Musk’s xAI sued Minnesota on Monday challenging a state ban on “nudification apps” that can generate AI deepfakes, POLITICO’s Hassan Ali Kanu reports.

The Minnesota ban forbids businesses and platforms from enabling users to create explicit images from non-sexual photos. The law imposes fines of up to $500,000 per violation, and gives victims a right to sue businesses that allow such activity to occur.

The lawsuit filed by xAI alleges that the ban violates the First Amendment because it is overly broad, potentially capturing protected speech like imagery of people in swimsuits. The company “does not contest Minnesota’s interest in prohibiting the dissemination of artificially generated nude images of real people without their consent,” xAI said in the complaint. “But the statute Minnesota enacted extends far beyond that goal, exposing a wide array of protected speech to civil liability and government sanctions.”

Minnesota’s Attorney General Keith Ellison didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Pornhub’s online age-check offensive
item.description: Pornhub’s online age-check offensive
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Pornhub is urging lawmakers to rethink age verification. | Leon Neal/Getty Images

Pornhub has charged headfirst into debate over online age verification laws. The adult content company has blocked most access to its platform in 25 states and three countries instead of implementing age gating. Pornhub sent a letter to more than 300 state officials on Tuesday, lambasting the “performative, ineffective, and unenforceable age verification laws” that they helped to pass. The platform argues that age-gating rules should target device developers, rather than individual websites, to safeguard privacy and user safety. DFD spoke with Alex Kekesi, head of community and brand at Pornhub’s parent company Aylo, about the site’s stance on age verification. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

Was there a serious problem with minors accessing adult content before the recent advent of age verification laws, which made them necessary?

We're absolutely aligned with the spirit of age verification laws. We do think age verification is long overdue. If you're looking at it state-by-state in the U.S., or on a more national level in certain European countries, overall they’re tackling the problem in the same ineffective way: asking people to verify their age at the individual platform level. It's having an adverse effect where people arguably engage with even more dangerous content on [non-compliant] platforms.

Most recently in Missouri, we responded to the law coming into effect by not letting anyone access the site there. Then the response that the attorney general there made was that the law is a success because Pornhub has left. How is that a win if one of the websites that is actually taking this stuff seriously is not available to people who we know are not going to stop looking at porn? They're just going to go to much more dangerous websites to do so.

How has Pornhub sought to lobby and engage with lawmakers on age verification?

We've long communicated with governments all over the world to differing degrees. At a bare minimum, we've communicated that we'd be very happy to make our platform available for testing in certain jurisdictions. We are in this predicament — I can understand the hesitation that certain lawmakers might have from engaging with the adult industry. But the reality is that we are stakeholders in this situation.

What do you make of the California's Digital Age Assurance Act, which mandates age verification at the device level? 

We do have some faith that things are going well in California. The struggle right now … is that the age signal [i.e. information communicated from a device to a platform about a user’s age] is only limited to app stores. It's not being extended to browsers and individual platforms, which is what adult sites would need in order to make use of that device-based solution. Adult sites don't have apps.

Is Pornhub trying to offload kids’ online safety responsibilities onto device developers?

A lot of the discourse around age verification has been flawed by assigning responsibility only to one group. It's not just going to be the technology companies, it's not just going to lawmakers. We are ready to play our role, and we've been doing so for years. All of the compliance protocols we have in place — you're not going to find in other platforms. There's no one forcing us to do the vast majority of these things. There’s no law currently in place that says uploaders to the site need to have proof of consent and identity documents on file.

Why did Pornhub decide to block access for new users in the UK in response to the country’s Online Safety Act, which also requires age gating?

When the OSA first came into effect, we said that we would be willing [to cooperate]. We gave it a good six months, and had shared some of these initial findings to say we tried. We still saw that it was not working. We just saw that no action was taken, or that it was happening very slowly. Certain websites did comply, but the vast majority were not. We just could not continue operating in a jurisdiction where the law was simply not working.

So when Pornhub blocks access in a jurisdiction, is it a hardball tactic? You could keep operating there, but it's more of a statement of your opposition to an age verification law?

It’s exactly that. We've made the decision to comply by removing our offering from the market there because we don't feel it's responsible to put our users in a situation where every time they want to access our site, they need to use a third-party provider to exchange their personal information in order to access legal adult content.

The letter Pornhub sent to U.S. officials on Tuesday was pretty confrontational. Is that a change in tone from your previous policy advocacy around age verification?

It's a definite change of tone, because we realize that Microsoft, Apple and Google have the power to turn all of their devices on with a software update to be kid safe by default. The likelihood of them doing that without a legal mandate is slim to none. Lawmakers do have the power to make this happen.

In that letter, we call the laws “performative.” It's easy for a lawmaker to say, "I've signed this law that's going to protect kids." Well, how many kids are actually protected? How many people have not looked at age-inappropriate content as a result of these laws? This is data that still hasn't been shared with us.
A warning about the pace of AI

More than 1,100 researchers and executives at leading AI companies signed an online petition warning the U.S. government about how quickly the technology is advancing, POLITICO’s Gabby Miller and John Hewitt Jones report.

The petition, published Tuesday, calls on the U.S. government to back international efforts to develop technical and policy tools that can “deliberately pace” AI’s progress. “To realize AI's potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight,” the petition reads. “But each company — and country — is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration.”

Anthropic co-founders Jared Kaplan, Jack Clark and Benjamin Mann, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Google staff research scientist Laura Weidinger and Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao were among those who signed on.
U.S. halts imports of advanced robots

The Federal Communications Commission announced restrictions on Tuesday to suspend imports of advanced mobile robots like humanoids and quadrupeds, POLITICO’s John Hendel reports.

The agency also said that the restrictions would apply to power inverters that are commonly used to connect solar energy to the electrical grid. The move only applies to new models of the foreign-made technology — the use and sale of previously authorized models is still permitted. Producers of the relevant devices can also request conditional approval for new models from the Pentagon and Department of Homeland Security via an FCC application process.

The FCC’s move appears to be consistent with the Trump administration’s aims to restrain AI competition from China and the clean energy sector that the country dominates.

“Following President Trump’s leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America’s critical supply chains and, with today’s action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that,” Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement.
