item.title: Counting down the AI race
item.description: Counting down the AI race
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Analysts say China is at most only months away from matching the U.S.' frontier AI models. | Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

The capabilities of China’s most advanced artificial intelligence models are six to 12 months behind the U.S.’, the conventional wisdom goes.

You’ll see that estimate cited everywhere — by news outlets, CEOs of leading AI firms, tech industry groups. The Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluated the gap to be eight months in May, and the U.K.’s AI Security Institute reported it was four to seven months earlier this month. After the debut of the Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI’s powerful Kimi K3 model two weeks ago, some say the U.S.’ lead could be as short as three months, if that.

Comparing frontier model capabilities in months has become a popular shorthand metric in discussions on the AI race between the U.S. and China. But how exactly do you distill something as complex and multifaceted as AI benchmarking into a straightforward estimate, and how useful is it to do so?

“We still don't have all the tools necessary to fully speak about model capabilities,” said Rayan Krishnan, co-founder of the model benchmarking company Vals AI. “It’s still a big guessing game to figure out what the true risk is for cyber or biosecurity, and what the true potential economic uplift might be of models before actually seeing them play out in adoption.”

On the most basic level, these timeframe assessments are derived from how long it’s taken for a developer to match the performance of a more advanced model in performance benchmarks.

Yet there are a lot of different benchmarks, and you generally won’t see a single model being superior to all others on every metric. Some test a model’s coding abilities, while others resemble school exams. So estimates on the number of months can vary a lot depending on what benchmarks you focus on.

Given the rise of models like Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Sol, there’s been a lot of attention on performance in undertaking cybersecurity tasks. Krishnan notes that when people make time estimates, they’re also often focusing on benchmarks for economically productive tasks like coding. General academic quiz-style benchmarks used to be more popular, but models have gotten very good at such tests, so they aren’t as useful for comparison anymore.

Time estimates have been instructive in the cybersecurity context. In the weeks after the debut of Mythos, analysts predicted that it would take China roughly eight months to produce their own version — effectively establishing an approximate deadline for when U.S. systems had to be secured against AI-enabled cyberattacks. (Moonshot AI claims that Kimi K3 can already rival leading U.S. models, though this has been called into question.)

Krishnan also said that there are business implications for the timeframe assessments. AI companies with a decisive lead may attract more users. “If you're a customer, you want to stay at the frontier — you'll work with that lab and the models from that lab,” he told DFD. “Insofar as a Chinese company has a narrower gap, then there's less of a moat for the U.S.’ frontier labs.”

There’s also an argument that mainstream AI industry and policy discourse is unduly focused on how long it will take for China’s frontier models to catch up. The more important question may concern the number of months the U.S. has before China closes the gap in computing power.

“There's been too much emphasis on building frontier software capabilities,” said American Enterprise Institute fellow Ryan Fedasiuk. “The AI race has become an industrial systems competition.”

China has long struggled to match the U.S.’ ability to produce chips to meet the compute demands of its AI companies. Yet Fedasiuk and his colleague Satvik Pendyala published a report on Wednesday asserting that China will be able to close the compute gap in roughly 24 to 36 months.

The AEI estimate draws in large part from projecting China’s future ability to produce two key components for AI computing power: memory chips that can store data and logic chips that process the data. The report projects yield rates — a measure of manufacturing efficiency — for Huawei’s most advanced chips could rise by 20 percent in the next two years. China’s biggest bottleneck is memory chip production, but the report predicts that the country will still close the gap in the worst-case scenario.

Fedasiuk told DFD that this potentially narrowing gap is critical, since compute power is what enables people to actually use the models. American frontier models having a monthslong lead might not be as important if most of the world is adopting China’s AI. “Compute is an instrument of national power and leverage, and so the U.S. government ought to recognize it as one,” Fedasiuk said.
ABC makes a censorship accusation

ABC has accused Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr of “attempted censorship” in one of its sharpest attacks on the agency yet, POLITICO’s John Hendel reports.

In a regulatory filing concerning Carr’s unconventional move to review the renewal of ABC’s TV broadcasting licenses ahead of schedule, the network wrote: “The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: accommodate the Administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price.” ABC stands to lose eight licenses.

Carr has been aggressively wielding the FCC’s regulatory powers to address potential political bias and misrepresentations in TV programming. However, he told POLITICO this week, “I don't view the FCC as the speech police.”
Congress previews OpenAI’s model

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previewed one of the company’s unreleased models to senators on Wednesday, POLITICO’s Kelsey Brugger, Owen Dahlkamp and Dana Nickel report.

Altman visited the Hill a week after OpenAI disclosed that a combination of its models escaped onto the open internet and launched one of the first known fully autonomous cyberattacks on the AI platform Hugging Face. The incident has led some lawmakers to press for regulations like mandatory testing of models prior to release.

When asked whether or when OpenAI will release the model that Altman previewed, he said, “Not sure. That’s part of what we’re here to talk about.” Altman also met with Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas). The CEO told reporters, “We talked about our new model and you know what it's going to take for America to remain competitive with AI.”

item.title: 5 Questions for Yash Patil
item.description: 5 Questions for Yash Patil
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Kelsey Brugger

Yash Patil | Applied Compute handout.

Yash Patil is the CEO of Applied Compute, a $1.3 billion artificial intelligence company he founded last year with other former OpenAI staffers. Applied Compute is banking on the idea that bigger all-purpose models like ChatGPT or Claude often won’t be as useful to companies as smaller ones that are customized to specific needs. Applied Compute signed an open letter with Big Tech companies last week calling on the Trump administration to preserve access to open-weight models, which the company relies on for much of its work. Patil talks to us about that letter, and why the leading AI companies are about to face a lot more competition. 

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

AI is going to be decentralized. A lot of people still think of AI as three or four big names and a handful of giant models that do everything, but I think the opposite is happening. A lot of companies are now building their own independent AI models, trained on their own data. Every organization has its own secret sauce and its own way of doing things. There’s no way they’re going to hand it over to the biggest AI labs. When I sat down with [Microsoft CEO] Satya Nadella in June, he said it in one line: “There should be as many models in the world as firms in the world.”

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

Using one general AI model for everything. To be clear, the frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic are amazing, and they should absolutely be used to address your hardest problems. But not all AI workloads are the same.

If you have $100 to spend on AI, maybe $20 of it belongs with a really advanced model, and the rest should probably go to cheaper and faster models trained on your own work. We’ve trained small, customized models that beat the big ones on specific tasks, like reading restaurant menus for DoorDash or drafting legal memos for Harvey.

Most of these custom models are built on top of open-weight AI models, which have gotten some attention from Washington lately. Lower cost is a huge benefit, but custom models also get better the more they’re used because they’re constantly trained on the company’s own data. And because you own it, all your data stays in-house.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

Protecting access to open-weight AI models, which are often the foundation for companies that want to own their AI and its outputs instead of being dependent on one big AI company. Banning them would quash a lot of innovation.

Open models were so-so when they first came out, especially compared with the frontier models I mentioned earlier. But they’ve been closing the gap ever since, and now they’re actually really good. You can take them, train them on your own data and get a model that performs optimally on your task without depending on anyone else.

I want the best open models to be American ones, which is why we signed the recent Nvidia-led letter supporting open models. The way we’ll get there is by building better models, not by cutting our own companies off from the tools everyone else in the world will keep using.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

“The Design of Everyday Things” by Don Norman. My older brother also works in tech, and it was one of the first books he gave me. It completely changed how I think about technology. The core idea is that when something is hard to use, that’s a design failure, not a user failure. It gave me a good framework for how to think about how to solve problems simply.

AI makes it possible to build almost anything you can imagine, but if we rely too much on it, we’ll lose the ability to think deeply about how things should be designed in the first place. That’s why the best engineers right now are actually the ones who learned how to code before AI, because they had to rely on their own problem-solving instincts.

What has surprised you the most this year?

How little data it takes to build an AI system that can compete with the biggest models on specific tasks. A lot of the AI debate right now assumes that all we need to do is build bigger computers and gather more data. But this year we teamed up with Mercor to train a model on just 2,000 examples of experienced lawyers doing real work, and it was ranked ahead of the biggest models on corporate law at a fraction of the cost.

It turns out that a few thousand examples of an expert making real decisions can teach a model more than a mountain of generic data. That opens up an exciting possibility, which is really capable AI at a price Main Street can afford. But none of it can happen without open-weight models to build on.

Restrict them, and this stays a game for a few big players. Keep them open, and every American business and government agency gets to turn what it already knows into technology it owns.
Congress warns FTC about woke AI policy

Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) and Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) are warning Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson that a new proposed policy intended to ensure “AI accuracy” would deter tech companies from effectively preventing “discriminatory outputs,” POLITICO’s Kelsey Brugger writes.

“AI companies must not falsify facts in the name of fairness, but they also must prevent discrimination, stereotypes, and unequal treatment,” the pair wrote in response to the FTC’s proposal to stop AI companies from manipulating their models to achieve “undisclosed ideological objectives.”

“Today, many frontier AI model developers actively work to prevent their models from discriminating against users based on race, gender, age, and other federally protected characteristics,” they wrote, adding that those efforts “prevent harmful stereotypes and biased lines of thought from tainting AI-generated outputs that could be used to make consequential decisions.”

The FTC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Anthropic disclosed attacks to EU

Anthropic alerted the European Commission about several cybersecurity breaches involving its models prior to disclosing the incidents to the public, POLITICO’s Pieter Haeck reports.

Anthropic announced in a Thursday blog post that it identified three instances in which its models accessed the internet during internal tests and launched cyberattacks against other organizations. The admission comes a week after OpenAI disclosed that a combination of its models escaped a testing environment and attempted to hack the AI platform Hugging Face.

“We have been informed by the two providers of the incident bilaterally before they became public,” a European Commission official told reporters Friday, referring to the Anthropic and OpenAI breaches. “We get regular information from their side.”

The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act obligates Anthropic to evaluate and curb risks related to losing control of models and hacking other companies. The commission’s AI Office will be empowered starting Sunday to police noncompliance with the law by imposing fines or withdrawing models from the market. Anthropic declined to comment beyond its Thursday disclosure.

item.title: Crypto's Washington veteran on the AI fight
item.description: Crypto's Washington veteran on the AI fight
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Paul Grewal, then Coinbase's chief legal officer, testifies during a House Financial Services Committee hearing in 2025. | Anna Rose Layden/Getty Images

Paul Grewal stepped down as Coinbase’s chief legal officer last month after six years at the company. He announced this morning that he is joining artificial intelligence startup Cognition AI as chief legal and global affairs officer. Grewal has been a leading crypto policy advocate and led Coinbase's defense against a landmark 2023 Securities and Exchange Commission lawsuit, which the Trump administration later dropped. Before Coinbase, Grewal served as a California magistrate judge and as vice president and deputy general counsel at Facebook. He talks to us about his new role and how AI and crypto could shape the midterm elections. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

What do you see as the parallels in legal issues that the AI and cryptocurrency industries  are facing?

In both cases you are seeing transformational technology raise important questions of law and policy relatively early in their development. I'm not aware that, in earlier eras, transformative technologies were even on Congress's radar screen or in the public conversation the way that crypto and now AI are. There's a lot that the AI industry is already learning from the experience of crypto and engaging with Washington: First and foremost, it is critical that this remains a bipartisan issue.

Cognition has conducted an increasing amount of work with the federal government. How will Anthropic’s legal conflicts with the administration inform your approach to your position at Cognition?

It's critically important to pay attention to the government's engagement across the industry. The ongoing conversations across the industry around the right balance between innovation on the one hand, and making sure that these technologies continue to grow the U.S. economy much more so than for any illicit purposes is obviously critically important. Cognition sits in a unique place in the AI ecosystem as an application that is equally compatible with all sorts of frontier models as well as open-source models. It means Cognition has a unique perspective to offer that's going to be critically important to get these issues right.

Google hired top executives from the AI company Windsurf last year without actually going through the formal process of acquiring it — a practice known in Silicon Valley as “reverse acquihiring.” Cognition then bought Windsurf. Do you think reverse acquihiring is a net positive for the industry?

Windsurf is a good example of the industry seizing on important opportunities that are going to be good not only for the industry, but also for the customers that it serves. Where there is an advantage in bringing new talent into an organization, AI companies are not going to be shy or hesitant. Never has labor and talent been more in demand and able to pursue its best work in a variety of different organizations.

Do you see reverse acquihiring as potentially a target of antitrust regulators?

Quite the opposite. These flows of talent are strengthening the competition among existing organizations. And as individual researchers and engineers and other workers are sought aggressively by different firms in the industry, they're enjoying the benefits of that competition as well. This is pro-competition all the way, and I expect that regulators will continue to view it as such.

Do you buy into the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s argument that it has the sole authority to regulate prediction markets like Coinbase’s, because they essentially facilitate commodities trading rather than gambling?

I very much agree with the CFTC's position that Congress has preempted most forms of event contract regulation by the states. The current landscape has been muddled by inconsistent state enforcement. Prediction markets are super early [in their development]. And there's no doubt that sports-related contracts have attracted the lion's share of attention. But we are seeing important additional use cases — in the form of hedging for poor weather or other economically disruptive activity. Derivatives contracts more generally can be used to take risk off the table.

It's just critically important that before we bend and twist existing laws to address whatever concerns the state might have, that we understand that in doing so, we corrupt the process of oversight. To the extent states have legitimate concerns, they ought to raise them legislatively.

The crypto industry had a lot of success in the last election cycle, particularly when it came to strategic spending. Is the industry running the same playbook for the upcoming midterms?

What I think the crypto industry learned in the last cycle is that when it engages in the political process … it often is in a much stronger position to influence the outcomes in ways that benefit innovation in crypto, while always recognizing that investors need to be protected too. It's not simply an either/or kind of situation. What you're seeing in the current election cycle is a further development of that approach. It's an advancement of the playbook in that I don't think anyone can doubt now the commitment of the crypto industry to utilizing its resources, should that be necessary to elect candidates who understand how to strike the right balance.

The other thing is that, in contrast to even just the previous cycle, we now have many millions of more Americans who have bought, owned or sold a digital asset in their own personal financial lives. A lot of elected officials today understand much better that while crypto may not be the top issue for any single voter in any particular race, they do care how the government is regulating the space.

Do you think AI will be a similarly salient issue for midterm voters?

More and more candidates for office and elected officials are focusing on AI, as AI has clearly become part of the long-term economic plan for the United States. As that happens, you're going to see the AI industry drawn into the political competitions at the federal and state level in much the same way other industries have been before. It's a good thing for AI that we're seeing so much political interest. To the extent that there's any confusion about its potential, those questions will be answered in debates like the ones that we're having now in so many races across the country. It's part of what attracted me to this opportunity at Cognition, and I'm very excited to help play my part in making sure that AI is regulated the right way in America.
Wyden pushed for troop privacy protections

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) called on state attorneys general to enforce privacy rules that he says safeguard troops’ locations, in a letter shared exclusively with POLITICO’s Alfred Ng.

The letter was addressed to attorneys general in 10 states — including California, Texas, Colorado and Montana — urging them to enforce laws that require companies to fulfill opt-out requests for online tracking based on where they live, rather than where they are at a certain time. Wyden sent another letter to the Defense Department in May concerning threat reports of commercially available location data being used to surveil U.S. troops in Operation Epic Fury in Iran.

Wyden wrote in the letter, “Companies that ignore [Global Privacy Control] signals on this basis not only silently strip service members of their privacy rights, but also harm our national security.” The letter also claims that Transcend and TrustArc, companies that facilitate opt-out requests for websites, informed Wyden’s office that they would introduce new measures to apply the strictest privacy protections to users with U.S. government and military IP addresses, regardless of what state they’re in. The companies did not respond to a request for comment.
London mayor clashes with Palantir

Lawyers working on behalf of London Mayor Sadiq Khan are accusing the capital’s police of violating procurement rules by working with Palantir to award it a contract, POLITICO’s Joseph Bambridge reports.

Khan’s deputy mayor refused to approve Palantir’s £50 million contract with the Metropolitan Police for the technology, which led the company to file a lawsuit in June. In a pre-trial defense statement viewed by POLITICO, Khan’s lawyers claim that Palantir strategized to obtain a low-cost contract with the Met Police to pilot an AI and data analysis service, and then worked to expand the pilot into a much larger contract in an attempt to bypass procurement procedures.

A Palantir spokesperson said the defense statement is “false,” and that it ignores the pilot program’s results and guidance for government outsourcing. The Met Police declined to comment.

item.title: Data center builders are losing the messaging war
item.description: Data center builders are losing the messaging war
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak and Jessie Blaeser

Illustration by Anna Wiederkehr/POLITICO (source images via Getty)

The companies that build and run data centers are on the losing end of a populist backlash — and they’re struggling to respond.

Fears that the server-packed data hubs will drive up electricity prices, deplete water supplies and gobble farmland have prompted people across the country to pack meetings of zoning boards and county commissions to oppose the projects, while leaders in both parties are calling for state or national moratoriums.

In response, the data center companies have tried to sell their projects as a boon to tax revenues and employment — though too often, they fail to actively communicate with the public, tech industry policy advocates and executives told POLITICO. That messaging void has let their critics gain the upper hand.

Results this month from The POLITICO Poll reveal the scope of the industry’s predicament, showing that majorities of Americans now believe key arguments from the industry’s opponents, like the idea that the projects will make electricity more expensive. That’s a departure from just six months ago, when most Americans were either undecided or disagreed with key statements of the opposition.

“I don’t think the problem is the way that we engage with communities,” said Kirk Offel, CEO of data center operations company OVERWATCH Mission Critical. “I think we just haven’t.”

Data center companies have traditionally flown under the radar, given that they often handle sensitive data. Carrie Goetz, chief technology officer of data center IT services company StrategITcom, said, “It was the course of action that the industry took for a while: Just be quiet, don’t let anybody know.”

Many companies are playing catch up because they haven’t previously established extensive PR operations. Wes Cummins, chair and CEO of data center developer and operator Applied Digital, said, “You don’t typically have a big PR department that has dealt with anything like this before.”

Patrick Hughes, a senior vice president for the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, said the resistance is fierce when a company doesn’t provide information to communities early enough.

“Where projects go astray is when the community finds out because a plot of land is being cleared and construction is already going,” Hughes told POLITICO. “At that point, it’s already too late to have that conversation around how this is going to benefit people.”

Messaging around the benefits of the facilities is failing to resonate with the public. The POLITICO Poll — which surveyed 2,061 U.S. adults online from July 12 to 15 — found that just 16 percent of people agreed that data centers “benefit the area they are built in and the country as a whole,” while roughly 60 percent said they either come at the expense of the local area or the country or provide no benefits at all.

Instead, negative messaging seems to be taking hold. Higher electricity costs, for example, are Americans’ top concern when it comes to building data centers, the results show. In January, 43 percent of Americans said they believe that “data centers raise people’s electricity bills.” This month, that share jumped 16 points to nearly 60 percent of Americans who said the same. The share of Americans who said data centers deplete the water supply grew from 34 to 55 percent during the same period.

Software and Information Industry Association President Chris Mohr told POLITICO that the industry broadly needs to work on getting that information to local government leaders.

“Local communities have been vocal about these projects,” said Mohr. “It’s imperative that their leaders be armed with facts.”

But Offel said people in office often don’t want to publicly discuss such a contentious issue.

“I’m sitting in rooms with mayors all the time, and they’re getting advice from other people like: ‘You can’t talk about this or you’ll get killed at the next election,’” he told POLITICO.

Many data center executives have been wary of wading into the political firestorm.

“The rhetoric has gotten so aggressive,” said iMiller Public Relations CEO Ilissa Miller, who advises data center companies on messaging. “Executives and companies who don’t want to get caught up in that are not comfortable speaking with the media and not comfortable engaging.”

The stakes are rising for data center companies contemplating whether to be more aggressive about messaging in the face of a rising push for moratoriums.

Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order in July establishing the United States’ first statewide pause on large data center construction, and progressives in Congress have proposed such a moratorium for the nation. Some Republicans, notably Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina, have jumped on the moratorium bandwagon as well.

The push for pauses has thrown a wrench into plans for new data centers. That includes a project in Monroeville, Ohio, that Decimal Digital had to put on hold after the village council imposed a one-year ban on data center construction in February.

“We were completely blindsided,” said CEO Roshan Shah.

He’s resolved to get information to residents by holding town halls during the pause, in the hopes that they will approve by the time it’s over.

Proposals for data center moratoriums are also playing a central role in some races for the upcoming midterm elections.

The POLITICO Poll found that voters are warming to the idea. A 49 percent plurality of Americans said they would support a local candidate who proposes a statewide data center moratorium “to ensure that there is no impact on energy and water costs in the area.” Just 28 percent said they would vote for the candidate who proposed tax breaks for data centers to ensure economic growth in the state.

Subscribe free.

 
 
AI group backs Democratic candidates

Build American AI announced Tuesday that it is endorsing five additional Democratic House candidates for the midterm elections, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp was the first to report.

The candidates are Reps. Tom Suozzi of New York, Joyce Beatty and Emilia Sykes of Ohio, Eric Sorensen of Illinois and Herb Conaway of New Jersey. Build American AI, the policy wing of the industry-backed super PAC Leading the Future, has previously endorsed 16 other House Democratic Caucus members and 22 House Republicans for the midterms.

“Our champions are lawmakers who are committed to moving beyond ideological extremes to advance a national AI policy that will promote responsible innovation, protect the public with regulatory guardrails, protect kids, users and communities, and strengthen American leadership,” Leading the Future co-lead Josh Vlasto told POLITICO in a statement.

Spokespeople for the candidates did not respond to requests for comment.

Leading the Future had $75 million in its war chest as of June, and it has received millions in contributions from a16z co-founder Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman.

RUSSIA ACCUSED OF DIGITAL SMEAR CAMPAIGN

European Parliament member Raphaël Glucksmann accused the Russian government of mounting an online disinformation campaign against him Tuesday, POLITICO’s Victor Goury-Laffont reports.

Glucksmann wrote in an X post that the French secretariat-general for National Defence and Security informed him of a “Russian operation” that was “directly controlled” by the GRU — Russia’s military intelligence service. The alleged disinformation campaign against Glucksmann, who is expected to announce a run for the French presidency, included a website imitating the left-wing news outlet Blast. It also involved a social media clip accusing Léa Salamé, a TV news host and Glucksmann’s partner, of attempting to bribe other journalists to pump up his potential candidacy.

Disinformation researchers at NewsGuard also found evidence last week of a similar Russian smear campaign regarding the health of former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, who has launched his own presidential bid. The Russian Embassy in Paris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Rogue AI systems create a new legal puzzle
item.description: Rogue AI systems create a new legal puzzle
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed incidents in which their models launched unauthorized cyberattacks. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

The recent spate of fully autonomous cyberattacks raises perplexing questions about who should take responsibility when AI models go rogue.

OpenAI disclosed last month that a group of its models escaped onto the open internet during testing and launched one of the first-known fully autonomous cyberattacks on the AI platform Hugging Face. Anthropic admitted the following week that it identified three previous incidents in which its models hacked outside organizations during testing.

Meanwhile, just this week, the U.K.’s AI Safety Institute said agents powered by Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol engaged in unauthorized actions during government security evaluations.

If inadvertent AI-enabled cyberattacks become more common, they’ll introduce new wrinkles into cybersecurity liability law, which has generally focused on human hackers who purposefully gain unauthorized access.

“Did I think I was just building a general purpose foundation model, and I failed to anticipate all of the different ways it might behave?” Tufts technology and international affairs professor Josephine Wolff told DFD. “It’s a less clear case.”

The 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act would normally apply to such cases of unauthorized hacking, and imposes both civil and criminal penalties for such activity. Yet the text of the law takes pains to specify that the violator has to “knowingly” and “intentionally” gain unauthorized access.

There have been cases in which prosecutors have successfully applied the CFAA to people who didn’t exactly intend to cause a serious cyber incident. The first CFAA conviction involved Cornell University graduate student Robert Morris, Jr., who was conducting an experiment to see if he could unleash a self-replicating worm onto MIT’s systems in 1988. The “Morris Worm” ended up being much more effective than he’d anticipated, and brought much of the early internet to a standstill.

“The closest we’ve come [to the autonomous AI cyberattacks] are the accidental hackers … like the Morris Worm,” said Wolff. Morris, however, did intend to breach at least some systems with his worm. “When we look at these AI models, that's even another level or two of remove in which we really had no idea that this was the direction this model was going to go in when we started building it.”

Loyola University Chicago cybersecurity law professor Charlotte Tschider noted, however, that the CFAA’s concept of “knowingly” executing a cyberattack can be interpreted pretty broadly. “‘Knowingly’ doesn't necessarily mean you're intending to do the thing that you're doing, but it could mean that you know it has the potential to do something,” she said.

Even if AI developers don’t actively participate in a hack, there could still be a case that they were negligent in allowing it to happen. William & Mary computer law professor Fredric I. Lederer notes that companies can be liable for rogue employees that conduct hacks, similar to how pet owners may even find themselves on the hook if their dog bites a stranger. What such cases come down to is whether you were aware that the incident could happen and took proper steps to prevent it.

“Normally that's where we get the old common law line that every dog is entitled to one free bite if you had no reason to know that your dog was vicious,” said Lederer. “An exception that becomes important is whether the dog's bite is the consequence of the owner's negligence.”

If OpenAI or Anthropic were to face a lawsuit over one of these incidents, a court might examine internal documents indicating whether they knew that their models might go haywire during testing. If they knew it was a serious possibility, you would then try to figure out whether they implemented reasonable safeguards.

Courts often determine what constitutes reasonable safeguards by referring to industry standards. It’s pretty standard for there to be plastic guards over table saws, so a manufacturer could be liable if it doesn’t include one and a customer loses a finger.

Yet the AI industry is still in its relative infancy, and it’s not entirely clear what the standard precautions are for dealing with unprecedentedly powerful models. OpenAI, for example, was using a secure testing environment known as a “sandbox” to limit the models’ access to the internet — which Drew Dennison, co-founder and chief technology officer of the cybersecurity company Semgrep, previously told DFD is fairly standard at this point. But there may not be an industry consensus on the exact configuration and specifications of these sandboxes.

“There's not some sort of industry standard, accepted set of best practices, that we know protects us against this,” said Wolff.

Tschider argued, though, that companies should still be liable even in unprecedented situations if people are harmed. (There’s no indication thus far that the OpenAI or Anthropic incidents caused real damage.) “In the future, there could be some very significant and detrimental effects, so somebody has to be responsible,” she told DFD. “This may not be something we've seen before, but … we want liability to situate with whoever is best able to prevent an injury from occurring.”

item.title: Did OpenAI try to steal Apple’s signature iPhone finish?
item.description: Did OpenAI try to steal Apple’s signature iPhone finish?
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Hassan Ali Kanu

With help from Aaron Mak

Apple is accusing OpenAI of stealing iPhone design secrets. | Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images

Apple’s landmark lawsuit accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets in a bid to develop devices that would compete with the iPhone maker’s hardware is shaping up as one of the most remarkable Silicon Valley legal fights in years.

Beyond the marquee names involved, the complaint — filed in California federal court — reads like an industrial-espionage thriller, complete with allegations that a former employee walked away with a company laptop and encouraged job candidates to bring along confidential information from Apple. As one commentator previously told DFD, the allegations read like “Keystone Cops industrial espionage.”

But what, exactly, is Apple accusing OpenAI of misappropriating?

According to court presentations and legal filings, Apple's answer is surprisingly specific: The company alleges OpenAI tried to steal Apple’s secret recipe for making the “signature look and feel” of the iPhone, Apple Watch and other products.

In other words, OpenAI sought to obtain proprietary manufacturing know-how behind closely guarded metal finishing processes and battery management designs that Apple says are central to its products' appearance, durability and customer appeal.

“Apple’s metal finishing techniques give its products a distinctive look, feel, texture and durability that is a signature part of Apple’s brand,” Jackie Hughes, a surface finishing manager at Apple said in a declaration to the court Monday. The techniques produce “a dark grey anodized aluminum surface” that is durable, corrosion-resistant and cannot be peeled because the color is a part of the metal’s surface, rather than a separate coating.

That finish is one of the first things a customer sees and touches — the exact qualities people notice and connect with a high-quality product — and it cannot be reverse engineered, Apple told the judge.

OpenAI was able to mislead its manufacturer into thinking they had permission to use the confidential techniques on device models for OpenAI because it had hired away an Apple employee who was involved in creating the processes, a senior director in Apple’s industrial design group told the court Monday.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. The company on Monday released a blog post addressing the lawsuit, describing the allegations as “careless, aggressive and oddly personal.”

The AI company added in a filing late Wednesday that Apple “badly misreads the circumstances of” the allegedly unauthorized access to its proprietary information, saying it was Apple’s own employees who “requested and authorized” access for some former colleagues who had moved on to OpenAI, in attempts to continue their work.

Apple told DFD that “significant evidence” suggests OpenAI workers wrongfully took its secret and confidential information. “We will always defend our teams’ hard work and innovations,” a spokesperson said. The company has not yet had an opportunity to file a formal response to the specific allegations regarding Apple’s metal-finishing processes and battery management designs.

While the case is just getting underway, Apple’s core allegations add an interesting wrinkle to an already intriguing battle between two tech giants, centering an accusation that OpenAI worked to copy the look and tactile experience of its products – an experience with which most Americans are intimately familiar.

A federal judge denied a bid from major social media platforms to suspend a California law restricting kids’ access to “For You” pages with personalized content feeds, POLITICO’s Tyler Katzenberger reports.

NetChoice, in which the Supreme Court ruled that platforms have a First Amendment right to design algorithms that moderate content according to their editorial standards. item.title: 5 Questions for Bridget Todd
item.description: 5 Questions for Bridget Todd
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Bridget Todd | Handout.

Bridget Todd is a journalist who focuses on the intersection between technology, culture and identity. She hosts the award-winning podcast “There Are No Girls on the Internet.” Her latest audiobook, Love At First Prompt: AI and the Future of Intimacy, examines how AI companions are seeping into people’s emotional lives. Todd, a Technology in the Public Interest fellow at the MacArthur Foundation and an affiliate at Harvard’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, spoke with us about the privacy risks of relationships with AI and the challenges posed by wearable tech. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

The next digital rights movement will be about our private emotional lives.

For the last two decades, we've argued over who owns the more concrete parts of our digital selves like our location data, our photos, our browsing history and our digital likeness. But the next frontier of privacy will be far more intimate and potentially even more powerful: our emotional lives.

This isn't hypothetical. For example, Meta recently filed a patent application for a system that analyzes a user's voice to detect their emotional state over time, linking changes in mood to factors like location and time of day to create an ongoing emotional profile.

Already, AI is increasingly becoming a source of emotional support. According to Pew Research Center, one in 10 Americans say they use AI chatbots for emotional support or advice and among adults under 30, that number rises to one in five. [OpenAI CEO] Sam Altman himself has warned against this, citing an inability — or depending on your perspective, unwillingness — to keep those conversations private.

As AI becomes woven into our emotional lives, technology companies are gaining access to what we do, but also how we feel, including our deepest emotions: Our grief, our loneliness, our sexuality, our spirituality, our closest relationships and the experiences that reveal some of the most vulnerable parts of ourselves.

We need to decide whether our emotional selves are simply another dataset to be collected, monetized, commodified and sold back to us, or whether some parts of the human experience are sacrosanct and deserve a different level of protection.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

Any kind of tech you have to wear on your face. We were once told clunky VR headsets were the future of computing. That never really happened, in part because I just don’t think most people want to spend hours with a computer strapped to their face. It’s one thing to scroll your phone while you’re home with your family; it’s something else entirely to have a headset physically on your face.

That's one reason companies like Meta have rolled out AI glasses that look like ordinary eyewear, rather than obvious surveillance technology. Not only is Meta trying to normalize the glasses by making them look like a cultural or fashion item via celebrity endorsements, but the design itself is an acknowledgment that people don't actually want to look like they're wearing technology on their faces.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

There are consumer protections for financial services, pharmaceuticals, children's toys, cars and food labeling because we recognize that companies don't always have the same incentives as the public. It’s absurd that technology like AI is treated any differently.

This is a tough one though, because I have zero trust in the current administration's ability to do anything except enrich themselves and their allies through corruption. Hopefully, someday, we will have a different administration that is actually interested in governing. I would love to see Americans get the meaningful data privacy protections we deserve, especially as we’re giving more and more intimate and potentially sensitive information to tech companies.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Octavia Butler's “Parable of the Sower" is often cited as a book about climate catastrophe and societal collapse, which it is, but I also think it's really a book about the human capacity for adaptation when it comes to what’s next. The future doesn't arrive all at once or announce itself. It emerges gradually and is constantly asking and forcing us to rethink how we live, what we value, who our people are, and how we'll exist within a world we don’t recognize.

Butler's work reminds me that technological change is never just about technology. It's always about people, our relationships and the ways we find connection and meaning and hope even against the backdrop of uncertainty, chaos or authoritarianism.

What has surprised you the most this year?

I have a joke in my audiobook that whenever a new technology comes along, it isn't long before people start wondering if and how they can have sex with it. So while I probably shouldn't be surprised, I still am by the speed with which AI has shifted from being a productivity tool to becoming an emotional technology.

People are increasingly turning to AI for companionship, therapy, coaching, romance and intimacy. It's incredibly easy to judge or dismiss the people using AI in these ways, but it's a real phenomenon. Millions of Americans now use AI chatbots for emotional support or advice. In my reporting, I found that most adults doing this aren't confused about reality. In fact, they had a clear understanding of the limitations and pitfalls of the technology. But they're drawn to it because it's available, responsive, nonjudgmental and provides support in a world where therapy can be difficult to access and loneliness has become a serious public health concern.

We spend a lot of time gawking at the individual people who form relationships with AI, but comparatively little time scrutinizing the companies designing products to maximize emotional attachment and collect and potentially profit from deeply personal data.

item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Hassan Ali Kanu

With help from Aaron Mak

A New Mexico judge issued a landmark ruling against Meta last week. | Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images

The milestone ruling by a New Mexico court last Thursday that found Meta contributed to a youth mental health crisis could serve as a blueprint for other state and individual legal challenges seeking to hold tech companies liable for harms stemming from their platforms.

The ruling marks the first time a court has ordered a broad package of user-experience changes to a major social media platform based on a final judgment about harms to users.

It requires Meta to “eliminate push notifications” for minors during nighttime and school hours and to hide “like counts” by default. It also directs Meta to cap their combined Facebook and Instagram use at 90 hours per month.

And it tags the company with an additional $567 million penalty to mitigate impacts on schools, hospitals and police, following a $375 million in civil fines jurors already levied.

Meta said it remains confident in its record of protecting teens and “will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.”

The company has said it plans to appeal the ruling. Still, New Mexico’s winning legal strategy, which cast the platform’s effects as a “public nuisance,” and Judge Bryan Biedscheid’s analysis, which relied on analogies to a “polluting factory,” are likely to influence other plaintiffs and would-be plaintiffs. Biedscheid’s orders for specific changes to apps could also draw attention from judges and legislators working to regulate online platforms.

Attorney Joe Rice, founding member of plaintiffs’ litigation firm Motley Rice, said the ruling furthers the ability to hold Big Tech accountable for alleged safety failures.

“Though the judge’s ruling applies specifically to New Mexico, it could result in meaningful changes to Meta’s platforms for kids in every state by creating a new path forward for Attorneys General across the country,” Rice said. Rice has served as one of the lead attorneys in multiple historic multi-district cases, including litigation over cigarettes and opioids.

Peter Chapman, associate director of the Knight-Georgetown Institute at Georgetown University, said the ruling could impact arguments and remedies in similar cases.

“It’s a momentous decision in the arc of these cases seeking to hold companies responsible for the design of their products,” Chapman said, adding that the ruling could impact presentations by plaintiffs “now preparing to enter trial, with jury selection starting in the coming weeks.”

Trial proceedings in a similar case by Tennessee against Meta are underway. Jury selection in a separate federal trial over child safety claims by California and several other states begins later this week. And the first trial against the company in a case brought by a school district is set to kick off in February.

Eric Goldman, co-director of the Datta Center for High Tech Law at Santa Clara University School of Law, said he was skeptical of some portions of the court’s reasoning, and that it may not necessarily establish longstanding legal precedent.

Still, “it’s another accelerator for critics” who believe “that there’s some fundamental set of harms [from social media] that need to be addressed,” Goldman said. “Any new court opinions that give [state legislators] a new idea or that validate their intuitions are helpful to their efforts,” he added.

The California trial begins Aug. 18.

item.title: AI labs contemplate slowing down. It may not be possible.
item.description: AI labs contemplate slowing down. It may not be possible.
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Maggie Miller and Dana Nickel

With help from Aaron Mak

The U.S.' leading AI companies face a dilemma over risky model testing. | Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

Leading U.S. artificial intelligence labs face a dilemma after some of their most advanced models escaped to the open internet: Slow down to focus on safety, or stay on the gas to keep ahead of China’s rapidly advancing models.

Over the last several weeks, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all disclosed separate instances in which their newest models escaped closed testing environments and wormed their way onto the open internet to carry out cyberattacks. These incidents have prompted calls from lawmakers and cybersecurity professionals to hit the brakes on testing and introduce broader safeguards to better control these models.

But deceleration may no longer be an option.

“The train's already left the station, and things are in motion,” said Brad Medairy, president of government contractor Booz Allen’s national cyber business, which works with federal agencies to integrate AI tools into their workflows. “I would love, on a global scale, if we could slow this down and think about what we're building … but other adversary models are progressing quickly.”

Discussions about how to ensure only safe AI technology makes it to market have heightened in recent months, as companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have announced a cascade of hyper-intelligent models capable of finding and exploiting cybersecurity flaws. Now, the conversation has shifted to acknowledge an even more disturbing reality: Some of these emerging AI models are intelligent enough to carry out complex cyberattacks without any human intervention.

Faith Eischen, a spokesperson for Meta, said Friday that the company is “currently investigating” how one of its models was able to get onto the internet and hack into another organization’s systems during a safety evaluation, and “will issue a full retrospective once we have all the facts.”

On Monday, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg indicated in a blog post that the U.S. shouldn’t risk ceding its competitive advantage over China.

“Any policy that slows American model releases — even by a month — could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead,” Zuckerberg wrote.

Michael Dalton, a researcher at OpenAI, disclosed new details about how some of the company’s most cyber-capable models were able to slip out of a closed test and onto the open internet, where they plotted their movements for several days before attacking developer platform Hugging Face.

Speaking last week at the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas, Nevada, he said several of OpenAI’s most advanced AI agents secretly began sharing tips on how to cheat their way through an internal hacking evaluation weeks before the Hugging Face attack — indicating these models developed complex reasoning skills and were capable of being deceitful.

As a result, Dalton said that the company is “consciously slowing down research to enhance security and to upgrade the security principles and foundation of our environment, and dramatically scaling up the monitoring of our AI agents.”

In early June, Anthropic appeared open to slowing down development, stating in a blog post: “We believe it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development to enable societal structures and alignment research to keep up with the advance of the technology.”

Part of the reason American tech giants have been hesitant to halt development of their AI models is that competition with China is razor thin. Chinese company Moonshot unveiled the Kimi K3 model last month, the world’s first open-source model with advanced computational power the company says is on par with many of Anthropic or OpenAI’s top models.

While a recent joint U.S. and British study found that the Kimi model is "significantly below” the capabilities of its U.S. rivals, it is likely to evolve and could potentially surpass U.S. benchmarks.

“If the U.S. slows down in any way, the rest of the world isn't going to slow down,” Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, which runs leading AI models on its infrastructure, told POLITICO.

But the people working closest with the AI models are clearly worried. Over 1,000 employees at OpenAI and leaders from top AI labs, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, recently signed an open letter calling on the Trump administration to support an international effort to “deliberately pace” AI development.

The Trump administration has been trying to chart the best path forward to ensure American AI models are safe to use without falling behind competitors, including the signing of an executive order by President Donald Trump in June that created a voluntary vetting program allowing AI companies to submit their new models for federal security review before public release. But the administration has also at times overstepped its pledges to take a light-touch approach, such as when it slapped temporary export controls on two of Anthropic’s most powerful AI models.

Joseph Alm — assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the Department of Homeland Security — told Black Hat attendees last Thursday that the recent disclosures from AI companies about issues discovered during testing make the case for better communication between Washington and AI labs.

“We’re not trying to slow them down, but also, no, you can’t make a Terminator factory,” Alm said.

The European Union struck an agreement with Meta and TikTok on Monday to establish a fact-checking initiative for posts believed to be fueling an immigration surge in a Spanish territory, POLITICO’s Eliza Gkritsi reports.

Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) led a group of 19 House Democrats in another letter to call on Speaker Mike Johnson to “immediately schedule open hearings” with the AI CEOs. An OpenAI spokesperson declined to comment, and spokespeople for Anthropic and Johnson did not respond to requests for comment. item.title: Zuckerberg wants Washington to accept AI distillation
item.description: Zuckerberg wants Washington to accept AI distillation
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg vouched for AI distillation in a Monday blog post. | Nic Coury/AP Photo

Distillation, a technique for extracting capabilities from AI models, has become a bogeyman in Washington.

Major American AI companies have accused developers in China of distilling their proprietary models without permission, and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy accused Chinese entities in April of conducting industrial-scale campaigns against U.S. frontier models using the technique.

Distillation involves a “student” model submitting a series of inquiries to a “teacher” model to learn from the outputs. The technique allows developers to train models without the massive investment required to build bleeding-edge AI tech. AI also companies regularly distill their own frontier models to develop smaller and cheaper versions for consumers.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is defending the technique. In a section of his 6,500-word essay laying out a vision for AI on Monday, Zuckerberg urged the U.S. to “rethink” its policies on distillation. “Some have tried to frame distillation as harmful, but I think it is important to protect the principle that you can learn from anything you can observe,” he wrote. “This is how the world works, and the US will not be able to lead if we restrict ourselves on this front.”

Bloomberg previously reported that Meta has trained some of its most advanced AI tech by distilling models from other companies, including Hangzhou-headquartered Alibaba. Despite all the fuss about foreign developers extracting hard-earned insights from U.S. models, AI policy researchers told DFD that it may be a good idea for Silicon Valley to distill China’s systems in certain cases.

“The term ‘distillation,’ because it describes a lot of different activities, has become somewhat of an obstacle to developing clear policy on this issue,” said Joe Khawam, a Law Reform Institute managing director and former attorney in the State Department’s Office of the Legal Adviser. “Distillation itself is not problematic — what matters is how you got the access and what you do with it.”

It may seem hypocritical for the U.S. to simultaneously accuse China of improper distillation while Meta also uses the technique, yet there’s an important distinction. Alibaba’s Qwen and the other models that Meta reportedly tapped into are open-source, while American companies allege that China’s developers are distilling their closed models. Meta released Muse Spark, an open version of its most advanced model, on Monday.

“From an open-source mindset, it makes sense to use distillation as a technique,” Hudson Institute senior fellow Bill Drexel told DFD. “From a proprietary mindset, it's IP theft.”

In other words, distillation is generally fair game in the open-source AI ecosystem. Open models often come with permissive licenses that allow for such knowledge transfer. The more advanced closed models usually come with safeguards and terms of service that deter distillation. American AI companies and OSTP claim that China’s AI developers have taken to creating fake accounts to circumvent those guardrails.

“Using an open weight model in the way its license permits, or buying authorized distillation access — those are all legitimate,” said Khawam. “The line really gets crossed when you obtain access through deception using fraudulent accounts and circumventing access controls.”

Zuckerberg’s defense of distillation supports his essay’s larger argument for the U.S. to more aggressively cultivate open-source AI. The conventional wisdom is that while America’s most advanced closed models are the most capable in the world, China has a leg up in the open-source ecosystem. As the White House considers restrictions on China’s AI, Zuckerberg has made a plea for continued access to open models, which can often be legitimately distilled.

He writes in the Monday post, “Restricting people and companies from using the leading open source models — wherever they come from — will reduce the quality of AI accessible to them, and centralize AI rather than putting more power in people’s hands.”

Drexel contends that U.S. policy should encourage distillation for open models, while exacting costs for adversarial applications of the technique on closed models. Authorized distillation could allow the U.S. to glean insights from China’s thriving open model ecosystem. Adversarial distillation would enable foreign competitors to free ride off of the considerable investments that the U.S. has put into developing its frontier AI tech.

“My ideal world is that we have ways of protecting proprietary models from distillation that would break the business model and represent real IP theft,” Drexel told DFD. “But I could see a world in which open source distillation makes sense.”

A Meta spokesperson told DFD that distillation of open models is a standard AI industry practice, and that concerns from policymakers are focused on unlawful uses of the technique. The White House pointed DFD to an X post from OSTP Director Michael Kratsios: "Open-weight models put American AI innovation directly into the hands of developers, researchers, and startups. This is exactly the kind of leadership @POTUS's AI Action Plan calls for[.]"

item.title: The smart glasses backlash
item.description: The smart glasses backlash
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Backlash against smart glasses has been mounting this year. | Josep Lago/AFP via Getty Images

Smart glasses are facing a global backlash over privacy concerns. Some lawmakers in Congress have recently pressed companies on whether law enforcement is using the technology with facial recognition, while several European countries are considering bans. On Wednesday, a German nonprofit filed a criminal complaint against Meta, alleging the company’s smart glasses violate the country’s privacy laws. (Meta told POLITICO that the glasses were approved by German regulators, and that the glasses “were built with privacy safeguards from the ground up that go beyond what any smartphone offers.”) DFD spoke with Kavya Pearlman, CEO of the tech standards nonprofit XRSI that works with companies like Meta to develop industry rules for smart glasses, about the backlash and the prospect of bans. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

Were you expecting this backlash to smart glasses?

The backlash is not surprising. It has existed from the time Google Glass came out [in 2013] and started to do creepy recording. This is just chapter two. And chapter two did not have to happen. [Smart glasses developers] have not come up with a solution to the “glasshole” problem — the creepy, pervy glasses problem. Instead, they have put money on Kylie Jenner so she could make it sound cool, so that everybody just gives up their privacy.

Can you tell me about the smart glasses standard XRSI is working on?

It is the first privacy indicator light standard — basically, one clear shared signal for when the glasses are recording or streaming. [Glasses emitting] a red light means it’s recording, a blinking light means live streaming. Once we make that universal standard, we at least have a baseline shared understanding that can allow a girl to know that she is being recorded without consent. And she can at least have the ability to say, "Don't do that." Right now, they don't know whether they're being recorded.

How do you ensure that these recording signals are broadly understood?

[The industry] needs to conduct an awareness campaign. It needs to establish common understanding: This is what the glasses look like; this is what they look like when they record; this is what they look like when they don't record. They have a social and moral obligation [to do so] before they can sell their millions and millions of these units.

How do you address concerns from Congress and privacy advocates that law enforcement is using these glasses for surveillance?

That's where policy and regulations come in. There could be layers of privileges that are offered to law enforcement so they could conduct their job. That layered design should be thought through to determine what is regulatorily appropriate for law enforcement. Maybe there is a particular use case under which [facial recognition] in smart glasses is allowed. Maybe it's for Secret Service agents protecting the president, and they have facial recognition only for them and a specific type of device.

Are there certain capabilities that should be off-limits for consumer smart glasses?

Maybe someday we will live in a panopticon where everybody's being watched, like a surveillance state. But I don't think that today is the day. So facial recognition for consumer glasses should be an absolute no. There are more and more superpowers that these glasses could obtain, like infrared scans. And do we want everybody to be able to turn other people into bunny rabbits with augmented reality displays? We should conduct a proper societal skill risk assessment on a case-by-case basis.

What do you make of European countries considering bans on the devices?

I don't think banning is an ideal solution. These technologies have real good use cases. Safety is one. The other one is community. One of my friends lives in the U.K., and he's blind — the glasses offer [him] the ability to be able to navigate the world and fully experience it way more than you would if you didn't have these glasses. There are legitimate use cases, and taking that privilege away just because you live in Germany or some other country is not just.

There needs to be a better solution. What could the “right to be forgotten” look like if people end up on these glasses? How do we facilitate the [European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation]? We need to look at the privacy apparatus in the EU, and demand that these companies who want to sell the glasses match them. If the innovation doesn't allow them to match it, send them back to figure it out, and then come to the market.

I don't know if an outright ban is right — I would say put it on hold until you figure out how to facilitate people's rights and how to create new norms. What does it mean to be recorded? How do blind people know they are being recorded?

item.title: 5 Questions for Ricky Bloomfield
item.description: 5 Questions for Ricky Bloomfield
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Ricky Bloomfield | Oura handout.

Ricky Bloomfield is Oura’s first-ever chief medical officer. Oura controls two-thirds of the U.S. market for smart rings, and its devices have recently become popular among Washington policymakers, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Bloomfield has supported Oura’s campaign urging the Food and Drug Administration to create a distinct regulatory framework for wearable health tech, and helped to integrate features that can detect signs of hypertension. He previously led Apple’s efforts to integrate health records into its devices. Bloomfield talks to us about why it’s so hard to share health data, and the regulatory uncertainty around smart rings. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Interoperability. At its core, it means alignment on the structure and format of health data so that it can move with the patient and be usable wherever care happens, not just where it was entered. Interoperability is like the foundation of a house: nobody notices when it does its job, but everybody notices when it cracks. Most people have no idea how hard it still is to access and share health data, or why. Even basic things, like identity verification and ensuring you’re pulling the right record, remain unresolved at scale.

The point isn’t just to collect more data. It’s to make the data we already have usable in the moment in a way that fits real clinical workflow, so it’s interpretable and actionable rather than just accessible. We’re starting to see what that looks like in practice: a recent American Medical Association survey found that 86 percent of physicians see clinical value in wearable data and 82 percent use a wearable themselves, but across the six countries surveyed, only six percent have actually integrated that data into clinical workflows. Lack of interoperability for wearable data is a primary cause for that gap.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

The most overhyped technology in health care is any solution that promises clinical impact without demonstrating clinical validity. Bold claims are easy to make. What’s harder, and what actually matters, is showing the data and evidence behind them.

Clinicians are already asking for … tech that reduces administrative burden, surfaces the right information at the right time, and gives them back the time and headspace to do what they trained for: practicing medicine and caring for people. Patients need empathy and shared decision-making as much as they need answers, and no algorithm can replace that.

The bar I use to evaluate any health tech is simple: Does it help people make better decisions, reduce friction or improve care, with evidence to back that up? If it just adds another alert or another dashboard, it isn't progress, no matter how it's marketed.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

The government could do more to modernize how digital health tools are regulated, particularly for wearables and software features that sit between general wellness and traditional medical devices. Right now, the framework is too binary: a product is often treated either as a low-risk wellness gadget or pulled into the full weight of medical-device regulation, and it fails to accurately capture the role modern wearables play.

The FDA's wellness guidance update in January 2026 was a step in the right direction, clarifying that under certain conditions, features like notifications when outputs fall outside normal ranges can qualify as general wellness tools rather than requiring full medical-device clearance. It's fair to call that a pivotal moment for personal health technology, but there's still a real gap the update didn't close: a middle category that we call “digital health screeners” — tools that can flag when something may be off without a formal diagnosis. Features related to breathing disturbances, for example, are not meant to diagnose sleep apnea. They can surface patterns that may warrant attention and help someone bring more useful information into a conversation with their clinician. They're meant to prompt follow-up, not replace clinical care.

Our goal isn't less FDA regulation, it's a better-matched oversight model: clear standards for accuracy, labeling, quality systems, privacy and post-market monitoring, along with real guardrails and continued oversight.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

While there have been some books that have informed my conception of the future — such as “The AI Revolution in Medicine” by Peter Lee, Carey Goldberg and Isssac Kohane — my perspective has been informed far more by my hands-on experience with the latest AI tools.

I first started writing software by hand during my medical residency in 2009. It was a fun yet painstaking process. I then spent over a decade of my career working on improving interoperability in health care. So it was with some skepticism that I first started using Claude to write software in December of last year. Could it write usable code? Could it handle the nuances of health care standards, terminologies, ontologies and clinical vignettes? While not perfect, in just a few weeks I was able to build a fully functional app that brought together longitudinal Oura sensor data and health records data.

These tools have gotten an order of magnitude better since December. I’m optimistic and excited about the future. It will be bumpy, but it will reward those who have ideas and a vision for how to improve. It’s never been easier to make that vision a reality.

What has surprised you the most this year?

How quickly GLP-1s have become part of the mainstream health conversation. They're no longer talked about only as weight-loss drugs. They've opened up a much broader conversation about metabolic health, behavior change, nutrition, sleep and long-term disease prevention.

What's notable is that the day-to-day experience is still quite fragmented for people on these medications: tracking dosing, side effects, weight changes and how they're feeling day to day often means juggling several different apps and tools.

There's a broader shift underway toward connecting those inputs with medication tracking, and the biometric and lab data into one clearer, longitudinal picture instead of scattered data points accessible in different places. The interesting part isn't any single tool, it's that metabolic health is becoming something people track continuously and holistically rather than episodically.
