item.description: Trump’s $100,000 paywall problem
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

President Donald Trump is being sued over a service offering paid early access to his Truth Social posts. | Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

President Donald Trump is once again expanding the frontiers of social media law.

Truth Social began offering a $100,000-per-month subscription for early access to Trump’s posts in July. The Trump Media and Technology Group, Truth Social’s parent company, advertised the service as a “real-time feed of the platform's most market-moving” content. But the Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a lawsuit alleging that the subscription scheme violates their First Amendment right to access the president’s posts.

Their claims aren’t entirely unprecedented. Several First Amendment lawsuits over the past decade have focused on government accounts blocking users, and legal scholars say last week’s lawsuit is the next chapter in this recently developed body of case law.

“We have this established doctrine that when government officials use social media to carry out their work, they are bound by the First Amendment,” University of Utah media law professor RonNell Andersen Jones told DFD. “Selling special access to the president's announcements on a platform that he owns raises novel legal issues within this framework.”

Trump laid the foundation for this doctrine when he blocked critics from his Twitter account during his first term. In the seminal 2019 case Knight First Amendment Institute v. Trump, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled that blocking users was unconstitutional as Trump’s account served as a channel for people to communicate with the government. The Supreme Court didn’t formally take up the case, instead vacating the decision as moot after Trump left office.

A handful of similar lawsuits have followed, including another before the Supreme Court, in which school board members and city managers blocked users and deleted critical comments on their social media pages. These cases are premised on the idea that if the public has a First Amendment right to speak out at a public forum like a town hall, it’s also unconstitutional to prevent users from commenting or reacting with emojis on a public official’s social media post.

Many of those earlier cases focused on determining whether the defendants were using their accounts in a government or personal capacity. Officials are allowed to block people on their private accounts, though it can be a tough distinction to make if an official is posting a mix of content about their personal lives and government work.

Yet Eric T. Kasper, a University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire constitutional law professor, told DFD the court is likely to quickly conclude that Trump is broadcasting official communications on Truth Social. Trump regularly makes policy announcements about everything from Iran to tariffs on the platform, and White House staff help to manage the account.

“In practice, it is an official account speaking on behalf of the government and it’s exercising that authority,” said Kasper. “That would be a difficult proposition to argue against for the defense.”

Another significant difference is that previous cases in this vein have involved public officials selectively blocking antagonistic users. The First Amendment prevents the government from discriminating based on viewpoint and content, unless there’s an exceptionally compelling purpose. The Truth Social service, however, is available to all users willing to cough up $100,000 — regardless of viewpoint. The plaintiffs themselves acknowledge this in the complaint.

“This is not about viewpoint or partisanship,” said David A. Schulz, director of Yale’s Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic, which is helping to represent the complainants. “It’s about not profiting off of your government job.”

Viewpoint-neutral restrictions on speech still need to advance some legitimate government purpose. Despite that lower bar, University of Colorado constitutional law professor Helen Norton says it’s hard to see what government interest this subscription program is serving. She told DFD, “If the huge sums of money are going to the president in his personal capacity, as the challenge alleges, that makes it even harder to argue that there's a legitimate purpose for making that happen.”

A Trump Media & Technology Group spokesperson accused “left-wing activists” of trying to “censor” Trump in a statement to DFD. “Information from President Trump is disseminated by countless platforms and news outlets, many of which offer subscription APIs,” the spokesperson said. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

“A president selling priority access to news he himself generates for the benefit of a private company he controls is so blatantly corrupt and unconstitutional that it would have been hard to even fathom just a few years ago,” Freedom of the Press Foundation chief of advocacy Seth Stern said in a press release. “Nothing could be more antithetical to the free, independent press than the president charging for early access to his public announcements,” said The Intercept’s chief legal officer David Bralow in the release.

Z.ai announced Friday that it will delay the release of the weights for its latest GLM-5.3 model by two weeks for additional cybersecurity testing. The delay is due to concerns about GLM-5.3’s increasingly powerful abilities to identify security gaps. “As we scaled post-training, cyber capability developed faster than we expected,” Z.ai said in the announcement.

Z.ai appears to be taking a page from the U.S.’s AI firms by deciding to delay the release of a model. OpenAI researchers said during the Black Hat cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas earlier this month that the company will slow down research and enhance security measures due to the potentially dangerous capabilities of its models. While Anthropic has not made a commitment to decelerate, the company announced last week that it won’t be releasing models more powerful than Mythos.

Apple will redesign its privacy feature for getting user consent for app tracking in order to resolve a German antitrust probe, POLITICO’s Jacob Parry reports.

The German competition authority had alleged that Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature treated third-party services differently from its own services in violation of competition laws. While Apple denied wrongdoing, it has committed to changing the text and formatting of the consent prompt.

item.title: Uncle Sam wants a few good gamers
item.description: Uncle Sam wants a few good gamers
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The Federal Aviation Administration is hiring video game players to be air traffic controllers. | Andreas Rentz/Getty Images

The Federal Aviation Administration launched a campaign in April to recruit video game players, with the aim of harnessing their skills in strategy simulators and first-person shooters for air traffic controller jobs. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced last week that the FAA has hired more than 2,000 gamers since then. While the FAA has faced workforce shortages in recent years, Duffy said this recruitment initiative has helped the agency achieve 94 percent of its hiring goal for 2026. DFD spoke with Michael J. O'Donnell, former executive director of the FAA’s Air Traffic Safety Oversight Service, about the useful skills these recruits could have and what types of video games may help prepare them for the job. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

Why might video game players be suited for air traffic control?

Lots of different reasons — the knowledge base that gamers have, the ability to operate software and equipment through gaming. The decision-making skills that they learn with gaming is helpful for air traffic controllers because it's looking at a radar scope. It's taking a display and calculating in your mind how you can solve the problem. So gamers are really good because they have the ability to do it quickly. They spend hundreds, if not thousands, of hours in a digital environment doing that kind of work. The FAA, to address staffing problems, was really quick to bring on people who have that proficiency already. Most of these candidates grew up in the gaming world anyway.

Did video gaming factor into your job at the FAA?

I did encounter gaming simulations. The Air Traffic Organization had a really neat training program where you would put gaming software on an iPad. It's basically an air traffic control game that was made specifically for the FAA. I remember taking an iPad and learning to control traffic on the train on the way home. I'm a gamer myself, but with an air combat game. Air Force fighter pilots like to get on those games to keep their skills up.

What other kinds of video games could help prepare people for air traffic control?

One of the tests for becoming an air traffic controller [involves] looking at targets on a screen and deciding if they're going to conflict — so being able to visualize what something's going to look like in the future, looking for patterns, being able to strategize on how you're going to mitigate a potential conflict ahead of time. There's a lot of strategy games that probably help in that area.

Not a lot of the gamers that they're hiring are probably air traffic control gamers. There are more popular games that offer the skill sets they're looking for — like Gears of War. You gain hand-eye coordination with that.

Given advancements in air traffic control technology, have the interfaces become more like video games over time?

Certainly in more modern facilities that have newer equipment. The new technologies that have come out in the past 20 years have really been a benefit. We call it layers of safety, whether it's airport surface detection radars or Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast technology where aircraft transmit their location real time on a screen. There are a lot more tools available to controllers, and gamers can understand that electronic world better.

But the visual work that's done in an air traffic control tower is hard to simulate. You actually have to get in a control tower and look out the window to see what's going on. Those kinds of skills are really basic, but still very important even though you have electronics helping you. You still need those visual skills and be able to discern the spatial problems outside the window.

Are there issues with traditional recruitment pipelines that led the FAA to recruit gamers?

There's a large pool of controllers who come from the military. Military recruiting goals are being met or exceeded, and retention is better than ever. That creates a bit of a problem on the civilian side, because normally you get a certain number of controllers who have left the military. Now that number is smaller because they're happy where they are.

This gamer recruitment initiative seems to be aimed at young people. Does the FAA need young air traffic controllers in particular?

They need to hire controllers before they’re 31, [which is] when the application window closes. It makes sense that they want to hire people in their 20s, who can be up and running before they're 31. … Gamers can get proficient quicker — their brain is just trained that way.

Are there any other types of nontraditional applicants that the FAA should consider?

The perception is that controllers are usually Type A males. Just like everything else in aviation, [air traffic control] is male-dominated. There may be younger women who think it's just a job for men — that’s not true. According to the Government Accountability Office, 85 percent of controllers are male, and 15 percent are female. That’s a pretty big disparity. There's probably a good number of women out there who could easily do this job.

ABC sued the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday in an attempt to block a review of its broadcast licenses, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp reports.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for D.C., alleges that FCC Chair Brendan Carr is violating the First Amendment by conducting a review years ahead of schedule that could result in the licenses being revoked. “Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the company argues in the suit.

An FCC spokesperson said in a statement that all broadcasters are obligated to operate in the public interest, including ABC’s parent company Disney. "Disney is obviously very concerned about the FCC’s proceeding, as evidenced by their ongoing campaign of disinformation as well as their decision to ask a court to stop the FCC from further pursuing matters,” the spokesperson said. “The FCC will continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead."

item.title: Why Adam Schiff wants to tax AI companies
item.description: Why Adam Schiff wants to tax AI companies
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Chase DiFeliciantonio

With help from Tyler Katzenberger, Joseph Bambridge and Nate Robson

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) speaks during a live taping of The Conversation at POLITICO's California Agenda: Sacramento Summit on Aug. 11, 2026. | Steve Jennings for POLITICO

California Sen. Adam Schiff wants to tax AI companies for their “disruptive” effects on the economy and the workforce, he told our colleagues at California Decoded, joining the likes of Gov. Gavin Newsom and other Democrats taking on a more populist tone about the booming industry.

“I would like to see the Congress identify what disruptive impacts should the AI companies pay for,” Schiff said.

He added that taxing income generated by the technology would “make sure that it's used to address and mitigate the impacts on work,” ensuring people have things like health care and retirement insurance while protecting “society from the transformation we're going through.”

Schiff’s comments come after Newsom has in recent months floated ideas like a national public equity fund to give all Americans a stake in the financial gains created by AI companies, or universal basic capital. It's the kind of share-the-wealth notion more often associated with progressives like Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, underscoring growing pressure across the political spectrum to confront the changes being wrought by the technology.

The anticipated blockbuster IPOs from OpenAI and Anthropic are expected to secure billions of dollars for investors and employees, further stoking fears about rising wealth disparities.

“I think we have to address the impacts that this is going to have, both on the nature of work and on the continuing problem we have with income inequality and with the kind of runaway concentration of wealth in the country,” Schiff said.

But Schiff — like Newsom — has been less inclined to go as far as supporting another tax idea that could hit the tech industry: the proposed billionaire tax on California’s November ballot. Schiff has declined to take a position on the initiative while Newsom has opposed it, highlighting the divisiveness of the idea within the party.

Schiff, meanwhile, isn’t confident this Congress — or even the next — can tackle kids’ online safety and said states should still be allowed to deal with pressing concerns about AI until Washington gets its house in order.

“I hope that we can at least do the low-hanging fruit, which is kid safety. But we don't have a good track record, and I certainly wouldn't want to preempt the states in the hopes that we're somehow going to improve,” he said, referencing attempts by the Trump administration and some Republicans in Congress to block state AI laws.

That leaves a major opening for state legislators in California. Chatbot safety, in particular, is an area where state legislators are on the cusp of making major gains this year, while Newsom has sought to get ahead of workforce disruption with a series of executive actions.

“Given our track record, we can't tell the states ‘don't proceed’ because I don't know how long it's going to take,” Schiff said.

Schiff has already been active on some of the AI impacts he’s concerned about: He co-authored a measure last year that would study AI’s workforce impact and make millions in grants available for workforce training and education.

The California senator is also sponsoring bills to rein in how AI is used in warfare and elections, as well as kids’ online safety measures, some of which he said he’s modeled on California’s existing age-assurance law.

Calling on Zuckerberg

Plaintiff attorneys expect to call Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg as a witness in an ongoing child safety trial brought by California and 28 other states, Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office confirmed to Decoded Tuesday.

“Mr. Zuckerberg himself chose profits over the safety of children,” Bonta separately told reporters at a press conference following the trial’s opening statements.

The announcement came after California Deputy Attorney General Megan O’Neill said during her opening remarks in the case that plaintiffs also plan to grill Instagram head Adam Mosseri and Antigone Davis, Meta’s global head of safety, during the roughly six-week trial. She accused Meta of illegally harvesting young kids’ data, designing Instagram and Facebook to addict kids and having “hid the truth” about platforms’ health risks.

Paul Schmidt, an attorney representing Meta, responded with a comparatively toned-down opening statement that sought to carefully dissect state prosecutors’ claims. He insisted Meta was forthright about safety and took steps to protect kids, such as implementing parental controls and teen-specific accounts, and that kids under 13 aren’t allowed on Instagram and Facebook.

“Every time [Meta] adopted a safety tool, they gave an announcement to tell people, ‘We have a new tool. This is how it works. This is why we’ve adopted it,’” Schmidt said.

Jurors on Tuesday also heard testimony from a key witness: Arturo Béjar, a former senior safety officer at Meta turned whistleblower on the company’s practices. He said Zuckerberg and other Meta executives failed to act on research showing its products were dangerous for kids, instead embracing a “culture of see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.”

Trump’s DOJ backs Musk’s xAI 

The Trump administration is backing Elon Musk’s xAI in a lawsuit against a Minnesota law that prohibits online platforms from allowing the creation of deepfake pornography and other explicit images.

Minnesota’s HF1606 is one of the first state laws to impose fines and allow victims to sue when AI tools generate sexualized deepfakes, regardless of knowledge or consent.

xAI has argued that the law was written too broadly and violates the First Amendment.

The Justice Department on Monday filed a statement of interest that largely adopts xAI’s arguments that Minnesota’s law is unconstitutional.

The law “sweeps up constitutional and productive conduct not prohibited under federal law because of the way Minnesota drafted (and apparently will enforce) the statute,” the DOJ wrote, saying the law theoretically applies to an image of a shirtless man in a swimming pool. The statute also does not give platforms a chance to remove images before imposing “crushing penalties” of up to $500,000 per violation, the Justice Department said.

The DOJ told the court that it supports Minnesota’s interests in prohibiting AI-generated sexual abuse material. Still, those interests should be balanced against First Amendment rights and the Trump administration’s policy of enhancing U.S. “global AI dominance through a minimally burdensome national policy framework for AI” instead of “50 discordant state” regimes, the Justice Department wrote.

The Trump administration also intervened on xAI’s behalf in a separate lawsuit by the NAACP. That case alleges xAI is building massive power plants near the Tennessee-Mississippi border without legally required permits.
